decisions.title: Optional embedder-supplied schedule row limit

context.text:
The limit and its meaning stand. Cron owns the row-limit policy; `CronStorage: Storage<CronRow>` atomically checks the limit and admits the new row in the same storage operation, so independent callers cannot race a separate count and write. This replaces the old bundled SQLite store's count check without weakening the limit.

[ADR-RUN-0013](architecture.md) keeps sc-cron a general scheduler: no two-row mutex, no global in-flight lock, and no beads-specific slot shape. Reloading schedules loads every row into memory; an uncapped row count is unsafe when schedules come from operators or configuration. Released applications must allow raising the ceiling without recompiling. sc-cron must not depend on `sc-config` ([ADR-RUN-0007](architecture.md)).

decision.text:
1. The scheduler accepts an optional row limit at construction (`max_schedule_rows: Option<NonZeroUsize>` or equivalent). **`None`** is the library default and means no row-count enforcement.
2. The limit counts **every row** in the schedule table, **enabled and disabled**. `replace` on an existing name does not change the count. Deletes free capacity immediately.
3. When the limit is set, adding a row whose name is new while the table is already at the limit returns the existing **`CronError::InvalidSpec`** (detail names the limit and current count). No new error variant ([ADR-RUN-0013](architecture.md) point 6 stays seven variants). Lowering the limit below the current row count never deletes rows; only new names are rejected until the count is under the limit. The check runs in the same store transaction as the insert.
4. **Generated sc-runtime applications** ship a sc-config key (name chosen by the template; default **`10`**) that the daemon reads at startup. Sentinel **`0`** or **`null`** in JSON means unlimited (`None` passed to sc-cron). The embedder maps config to the scheduler parameter; sc-cron never reads sc-config files.
5. **v1:** the limit is applied when the embedder builds or opens the scheduler (daemon startup). **v2 (optional):** a reconfiguration API (for example `set_max_schedule_rows`) may apply a config reload without process restart.

rationale.text: Owner ruling, 2026-10-27 (decision-sync-scheduling-at-api.md). The check runs inside the same store transaction as the insert, so two processes sharing one file cannot both pass it. The b-9 text that many names may each hold a blocking-pool thread is bounded for any consumer that sets the limit.

consequences.text: Sprint **`b-12`** implements the API, store count check, template default, and doc updates in `docs/sc-cron/` ([sprint-b-12-sc-cron-schedule-row-limit.md](plans/phase-b/sprint-b-12-sc-cron-schedule-row-limit.md)). beads-cache may enforce its own sync semantics; that is not sc-cron's default ceiling.
negative: Lowering the limit below the current row count leaves the table above the limit until rows are deleted, because existing rows are never removed.

groups.name: sc-cron reads the limit from sc-config
groups.description: sc-cron reads the application's sc-config JSON itself to find the row limit.
groups.why_rejected: sc-cron must not depend on `sc-config` ([ADR-RUN-0007](architecture.md)). The embedder reads its own config and passes the limit into the sc-cron API.

decisions.title: Benchmark campaigns in a controlled environment

context.text: Monty and sc-cron performance campaigns produce HTML and JSON under `site/reports/benchmark-<subsystem>/`. Timing data is meaningful only on a stable host. GitHub Actions runners are not a controlled benchmark environment and must not be treated as regression authority ([NFR-RUN-0005](requirements.md)).

decision.text:
1. Benchmarks are **automated procedures**: agents follow `.claude/skills/benchmark-run/SKILL.md` (the `/benchmark-run` skill), which drives `scripts/benchmark/` recipes (`just --justfile scripts/benchmark/justfile …`) and subsystem `campaign.py` runners. This is repeatable automation, not ad-hoc manual timing.
2. **Authoritative timings** come only from a **controlled benchmark environment**. The primary reference host is **`atmbench@rand-m5`** (SSH). Campaign JSON records git SHA, `rustc` version, subsystem, cases, and a **host label** (`SC_BENCH_HOST_LABEL` or hostname). Baselines in `baselines.json` belong to that environment class.
3. **Default PR CI and root `just test`** do not run benchmark campaigns or `benchmark-gate`. CI may compile ignored bench tests; it does not produce benchmark regressions.
4. **Publish preflight** verifies committed controlled-host benchmark evidence using `scripts/benchmark/check_release_evidence.py` ([sprint b-11](plans/phase-b/sprint-b-11-benchmark-monty-reports.md)). A developer first runs the fresh workspace campaign on `atmbench@rand-m5`, commits JSON/HTML and the regenerated index under `site/reports/`, and quality manager reviews the results and measured build. Hosted preflight does not SSH to the controlled host. It fails closed on missing or invalid evidence, skipped cases, baseline failures, or release source differing from the measured source beyond added campaign reports/index updates. Identical source after a squash merge remains eligible. First-release measurement requires neither a published SDK nor an installed prerelease archive; registry-only consumer proof remains separate. Existing release-candidate tag policy is unchanged.
5. The platform layout is multi-subsystem: `scripts/benchmark/<subsystem>/` and `site/reports/benchmark-<subsystem>/`. The first subsystem is `monty`.

rationale.text: Owner, 2026-10-27. Timing data is meaningful only on a stable host. GitHub Actions runners are not a controlled benchmark environment and must not be treated as regression authority (NFR-RUN-0005).

consequences.text: Sprint `b-11` implements the skill, layout, `benchmark-gate`, and the `benchmark-pass` entry in publish preflight. Operators coordinate access to the `atmbench` account; agents run the documented procedure.
negative: A release whose tracked source differs from the measured source beyond added campaign reports and index updates requires another campaign on `atmbench@rand-m5` before publish preflight passes.

decisions.title: Explicit Python and Monty hook environments

context.text:
The Python hook currently inherits the complete daemon environment. Monty
denies all OS calls, including its existing `Getenv` and `GetEnviron` calls,
while the compose child inherits the complete daemon environment. That is an
inconsistent capability boundary and has caused difficult identity/team bugs
when a daemon starts under one agent and later executes another agent's
schedule. The invoking agent process may not even exist when a durable cron
entry runs.

Environment variables are not uniformly secrets. Durable values such as
`ATM_IDENTITY` and `ATM_TEAM` belong with a schedule. API keys may instead be
daemon-wide inherited values, explicit schedule values, references resolved
by an application secret provider, or values loaded from an authorized
absolute `.env` file. The library must support those choices without silently
capturing host values.

decision.text:
1. `HookEnvironment` is one schedule-level contract for Python and Monty.
   Existing constructors default to empty. It contains ordered absolute
   `.env` sources and a name-keyed map whose operation is exactly one of
   `Set(String)`, `Reference(String)`, or `Clear`. A non-empty environment on
   a Rust target is invalid; trusted in-process Rust jobs keep the existing
   `Job` trait and may use the application/daemon environment directly.
2. `HookEnvironmentHost` is daemon scope. It names daemon-process variables
   that may be inherited, authorizes exact `.env` files or canonical roots,
   and holds an embedder-provided reference resolver. Every default is empty.
   The library never infers or captures an invoking caller's environment. The
   generated composition accepts a prebuilt host policy so an application can
   attach its resolver; config parsing never overwrites the trait object.
   Generated configuration exposes all three administrator lists:
   `allow_process`, `allow_dotenv_files`, and `allow_dotenv_roots`, each empty
   by default.
3. One immutable snapshot is resolved before `cron.stop` and shared with
   `cron.tick`: daemon allowlisted values first, `.env` files in declared
   order second, and schedule operations last. Set and a resolved reference
   replace prior values; clear removes a value. Missing daemon values and
   missing optional files are absent. Required-file, path-policy, parse, and
   reference failures fail closed before hook source runs. A reference request
   includes schedule identity, variable name, opaque reference, and the row
   deadline so the application can authorize per-schedule access. Resolution
   is deadline-bounded; expiration records `TimedOut`.
4. Python starts from an empty child environment and receives exactly that
   snapshot. Ambient inheritance remains possible only through an explicit
   direct-call `ChildEnv::Inherit`. Monty resumes only `Getenv` and
   `GetEnviron` against the same snapshot; missing or cleared names behave as
   absent and every other OS call remains denied. Source initialization is
   resumable only for environment reads so top-level `os.getenv` works while
   top-level registered host calls remain denied. Both sc_compose_run and
   atm_run children receive the snapshot and never inherit the daemon environment.
5. `.env` sources are full absolute paths, read at execution, capped, parsed
   as data rather than shell, and authorized after canonicalization so a
   symlink cannot escape an allowed file/root policy. Interpolation, command
   substitution, duplicate keys, and NUL are invalid. Authorization precedes
   missing-file classification; a missing optional file is accepted only when
   its expected canonical path is covered by an exact-file or canonical-root
   policy. Reference strings are opaque, persisted plaintext non-secret
   locators; the default resolver resolves none.
6. Explicit `Set` values are intentionally persisted as plaintext SQLite
   data. Values resolved from the daemon, a reference, or a file are never
   persisted. Every hook/provider-controlled detail or stop reason has each
   distinct non-empty resolved value replaced with `[REDACTED_ENV]` before its
   byte cap and before fixed codes/recovery, diagnostics, traces, outcomes,
   events, or persisted reasons are assembled. Stable codes, recovery text,
   metadata, and the canonical environment configuration write are never
   substituted; deliberate `Set` values remain plaintext schedule data. This
   covers Python output, Monty exception/return text, and both CLI adapters' stdout/stderr. Raw
   `HookOutput` remains available to a trusted direct PythonHook caller, but
   its `Debug` omits output content. Reference strings and provider error prose
   are never emitted.
7. sc-cron has not shipped a binary or package schema. Sprint b-17 therefore
   defines one first-release schema at `SCHEMA_VERSION = 1`. It validates
   the version and required usable columns/defaults/constraints/indexes;
   byte-for-byte SQL equality and exact column ordering are not gates.
   Incompatible development files are rejected without mutation with recreate
   guidance; there is no unreleased migration ladder to implement.
8. Environment names and values are UTF-8 and NUL-free. ASCII case-fold name
   collisions are rejected on every platform. An allowlisted non-Unicode
   daemon value fails closed rather than becoming absent. Runtime lookup and
   enumeration preserve spelling on Unix; Windows runtime keys are uppercased
   for both Python and Monty and lookup is case-insensitive, while persisted
   configuration retains original spelling. `MAX_ENV_NAME_BYTES` is 256,
   `MAX_ENV_DOTENV_SOURCES` is 16, every intermediate/final map is capped at
   `MAX_ENV_ENTRIES` (128), every stored/resolved value at 16 KiB, and the
   encoded block at 32,000 UTF-8 bytes. Python and both CLI adapter basenames are
   resolved to absolute programs from daemon launch policy before the child's
   `PATH` is cleared; relative program paths with components are absolutized
   against the captured daemon current directory. Secret-bearing `ChildEnv`,
   `ChildSpec`, and `PythonHook` debug output is value-free just like the
   environment model itself. The
   canonical JSON ordering and required first-release SQLite structure are
   tested as persistence behavior.

rationale.text:
Owner, 2026-10-28. A daemon's ambient identity/team is not the
invoking agent's context. Daemon-scope API keys may be exposed by name, while
each schedule must be able to set or clear its own environment and resolve
authorized secret references or absolute `.env` files.

consequences.text:
Sprint b-17 implements [REQ-CRON-0019](sc-cron/requirements.md) and
[NFR-CRON-0002](sc-cron/requirements.md), updates the generated daemon's
empty-default policy, and tests identical Python/Monty resolution. sc-cron
still reads no `sc-config` file and implements no secret backend. Applications
authorize agent-to-file access and provide reference resolvers. Monty
write-through `os.environ` mutation remains unsupported until Monty exposes
set/unset OS calls; sc-cron never mutates the daemon process environment.
Exact-value redaction mitigates accidental propagation, not transformation or
exfiltration by trusted hook code.
negative: Applications must authorize agent-to-file access and provide reference resolvers because sc-cron implements no secret backend. Exact-value redaction does not prevent transformation or exfiltration by trusted hook code.

decisions.title: General database commands ship on CLI, MCP, and HTTP

context.text:
Command paths need not be hand-written; default direct conversion requires no custom transform. Consumer-side generation remains permitted follow-up work.

The clauses "These commands do not add a command registry" and "Framework crates do not move rows" in point 4 bind nothing: the first does not forbid the shared command path, and row movement is deferred with synchronization.

sc-runtime is a set of crates and a template for deploying a new application that can use its database immediately.

The problem is how a new application with a store can use its database from the CLI, MCP, and HTTP before the consumer has written its own application commands, while the consumer can still remove that general public surface once those application commands exist.

decision.text:
1. A layout that has a store renders general database commands on the CLI, MCP, and HTTP. The set includes `delete row <table> <id>`. The commands are on by default.
2. An application command calls the same delete operation through its own CLI command, MCP tool, and HTTP route. The worked example remains `widget.create` and `widget.get`.
3. A flag removes the general commands from those three surfaces. A layout with no database renders none of them.
4. Row synchronization remains deferred. General commands may use the shared command path; they impose no hand-writing or future consumer-generator restriction.

rationale.text: Shared command operations keep CLI, MCP and HTTP behavior consistent.

consequences.text: Sprint `b-8` (deliverable 5) renders general database commands on the CLI, MCP, and HTTP for a layout with a store, including `delete row <table> <id>`. A flag removes them, and a no-database layout renders none of them.
negative: A generated store layout exposes `delete row <table> <id>` on its public CLI, MCP, and HTTP surfaces by default, until the consumer sets the flag that removes the general commands.

groups.description: A layout with a store always renders the general database commands on the CLI, MCP, and HTTP, and no flag removes them.
groups.why_rejected: REQ-RUN-0331 states that the consumer can disable that surface. The owner expects the consumer to disable the general commands and replace them with commands that have better UX and make a similar back-end call.

decisions.title: Cooperative cron operation and owned shutdown contract

context.text:
This contract is built on `SqliteScheduleStore`, which PRD-CRON-2 replaces with `Storage<CronRow>`. It has not been re-planned against PRD v2.0.

Phase C closes adoption gaps left after Phase b: existing cron Rust/Python/Monty registration remains usable through a public nominal logging facade and cooperative owned store/shutdown/query protocol. Cron is already ported; no new job kind or re-port is planned.

The problem is keeping the cron command request path nonblocking under NFR-RUN-0002 while a transport timeout or a dropped waiter could otherwise detach a blocking store mutation from the shutdown that is meant to bound it.

decision.text:
Phase C's default command intake completes this same pre-submission admission
contract with finite per-Scheduler capacity (default64, validated finite
pre-start override), immediate typed refusal rather than an unbounded wait
queue, and permits retained until physical completion after waiter cancellation.
Stop/cleanup remain independent; public commands cannot use private internal
paths to bypass capacity. Existing row-limit and
scheduled-job concurrency decisions are unchanged; custom operation/executor
providers retain responsibility for their explicitly documented overload policy.

REQ-CRON-0020/0021
and [the Phase C contract](plans/phase-c/compatibility-contract.md) specify the
public receiver facade, legacy-safe store admission, directly mutable real
monotonic budgets, tracked public CRUD/query, restricted generation-fenced
cleanup, typed expiry and actual physical ownership. This extends ADR-RUN-0013
without changing the bundled schema, existing Rust/Python/Monty targets or environment
policy in ADR-RUN-0016. It preserves ADR-RUN-0017's temporary nominal command
logging port rather than claiming upstream observability cleanup.

Caller absolute G/K permits equality. T=0 cancels immediately with no hidden
cleanup allowance or instantaneous-join promise. The shared real stop clock
is independent of schedule ManualClock; test-only forced expiry proves
propagation, while real-clock tests prove elapsed bounds. Unsupported stores
cannot enter cooperative mode, and provider overruns cannot become successful
bounded completion by dropping a waiter or emitting early status.

The framework charter retains custom ScheduleStore/schema and caller-owned
legacy integrations. The cooperative guarantees here apply to the standard
path and any custom provider explicitly implementing that capability. SQLite
hooks/TLS/interrupt are bundled-provider mechanisms, not requirements to use
SQLite in every application. Custom providers forward the live scope and
truthfully declare support or remain on the documented legacy path. C-5 proves
one application-field store example without changing shared Schedule/DTOs.

Human-approved commit clarification: G/K cut off new commit admission, not
universal physical commit/fsync completion. An owned commit_hook decision
briefly serializes stop/real-time/class/generation eligibility then releases
the controller lock before COMMIT. Admitted transactions may finish later and
remain physically owned. Report confirmed committed-late, explicit rollback
or indeterminate truthfully; expiry/Drop is not rollback evidence. No uncertain
mutation replay, expired-budget reconciliation or effects after physical
release. C-1 freezes typed TransactionOutcome/report/error policy, c-5 proves
the actual admission race and persisted state after join, c-4 proves packaged
behavior. This changes the prior strict physical-cutoff interpretation by the
explicit human decision, not a finding waiver or implementation PASS.

rationale.text: NFR-RUN-0002 and the existing service-hardening checklist section 7 motivate this operational bound.

consequences.text: C-1 freezes typed TransactionOutcome/report/error policy, c-5 proves the actual admission race and persisted state after join, c-4 proves packaged behavior. This changes the prior strict physical-cutoff interpretation by the explicit human decision, not a finding waiver or implementation PASS.
negative: When all command slots are taken, public commands are refused with `command_capacity_exhausted`, and callers reduce concurrency or retry later.
Shutdown does not guarantee physical completion by G/K. An admitted commit may complete late or end Indeterminate, and callers reconcile it through a separately authorized readback.

groups.name: Unbounded capacity-wait queue
groups.description: Public commands that arrive when intake is full wait in a queue until a slot frees, with no capacity limit.
groups.why_rejected: NFR-RUN-0002 requires a nonblocking request path. REQ-CRON-0021 instead specifies immediate fixed typed unavailable refusal when full, with no hidden capacity-wait queue, waiter registry or sleep/retry loop. The default capacity is 64, not unlimited.

implementation.text: Status as recorded: Approved Phase C target; implementation planned.

decisions.title: Optional standard cron command adapter and generated wiring

context.text: The problem is that each UI has no standard start/end/list JSON interface for cron schedules, while the scheduler core keeps no binary, HTTP/MCP routes or configuration-file loading. Phase C objective 4: an optional standard start/end/list JSON adapter presents the same operation/result/error to CLI, HTTP and selected MCP. Default-off generated configuration leaves core usable alone; explicitly selected configuration wires the real shared handler into the existing UIs.

decision.text:
The new optional
`sc-cron-commands` library provides common start/end/list JSON and canonical
Envelope errors, with Rust/Python/Monty execution options. DTO-only defaults
use serde/serde_json and defaults-off command; optional scheduler adds cron.
Core command and runtime gain no cron/adapter reverse edge. This explicitly
amends ADR-RUN-0003's workspace graph and the product-API restriction of
ADR-RUN-0013 only for the separate adapter: scheduler core keeps no binary,
HTTP/MCP routes or configuration-file loading.

REQ-RUN-0332 adds default-off generation selection and real selected CLI/HTTP/
optional-MCP wiring, governed by ADR-CRNC-0001. C-1 owns new manifests/shared

decisions.title: Shared typed storage and atomic operations

context.text: Applications and cron need the same typed storage contract across SQLite, Postgres and MySQL. Independent SQL and database-ownership paths prevent shared atomic policies and make engine changes affect application code. SQLite requires asynchronous admission to its dedicated high-throughput writer while generic engines remain independent of consumer tables.

decision.text:
1. The sc-storage crate MUST expose the shared asynchronous Storage<T> contract without dependencies outside the Rust standard library.

2. SQLite, Postgres and MySQL MUST implement the same Storage<T> contract.

3. Storage<T> MUST provide read, read_all and write operations for application-defined row types.

4. StorageRow MUST describe the row table, key, columns, encoding and decoding through validated row descriptors.

5. Consumer row types, schemas and migrations MUST remain outside generic engine implementations.

6. AtomicStorage::transaction(spec, producer) MUST commit or roll back its multiple row operations as one atomic unit.

7. Generic transaction handles MUST provide read, write, insert and delete operations across row types.

8. Each transaction retry MUST start a fresh owned Send + 'static producer future.

9. TransactionSpec MUST expose name and read-only/read-write mode through constructors and accessors with a non-exhaustive public shape.

10. Engine configuration MUST provide finite retry and deadline defaults.

11. The transaction contract MUST preserve the option of adding transaction-specific retry policy without breaking consumer construction.

12. Transaction observations MUST retain name, queue wait, run time, row-operation count and outcome.

13. Generic engines MUST quote validated identifiers and bind row values instead of accepting consumer SQL strings.

14. Storage failures MUST return typed StorageError values with stable code, retryability, source and recovery information.

15. Public storage functions MUST NOT panic.

16. The SQLite implementation MUST admit writes through a bounded asynchronous channel to one dedicated writer thread owning the sole write-mode connection.

17. The SQLite writer MUST batch admitted writes and send successful replies only after the outer transaction commits.

18. SQLite reads MUST use the reader workers of the same database implementation.

19. Only the dedicated SQLite writer thread MAY drive Runtime::block_on; reader workers MUST receive with blocking_recv without a runtime.

20. Async storage callers MUST NOT block or wrap storage submission in spawn_blocking.

21. A SQLite write transaction body that yields MUST roll back with a typed error.

22. SQLite writer failure MUST fail all admitted replies and close further admission.

23. CronStore<S> MUST keep its generic backend private behind the policy-checked CronStorage facade.

24. CronStorage MUST enforce active-name admission, configured schedule-row limits, generation fencing and multi-row mutations through atomic domain operations implemented once in sc-cron.

25. SQLite application and cron rows MUST share the application database by default.

26. Generation MUST reject cron when no database is selected.

27. Legacy cron import MUST preserve stored fields through an idempotent, read-only-source migration that refuses collisions atomically.

28. sc-cron MUST own CronRow and MontyBlobRow tables and migrations through generic row storage.

29. Schedule writes MUST reject Monty source that sc-monty cannot compile.

30. sc-cron MUST capture the compiled hook-session blob immediately after compilation and before any hook runs.

31. sc-cron MUST key each compiled-session blob by sc-sha SHA-256 of the source and the Monty dump version.

32. sc-cron MUST use a cached blob only when its key matches the authoritative source stored in the schedule row.

33. A missing, stale, corrupt or unreadable-version blob, or a loaded session missing cron_stop or cron_tick, MUST cause recompilation from source and replacement of the cached pre-run blob.

34. sc-cron MUST NOT persist hook run state in compiled-session blobs.

35. Backend factories and open options MUST belong to the corresponding engine implementation.

36. Application WidgetStorage, OpenWidgetStore and StoresView extensions MUST preserve generated identifiers and existing create, read and delete behavior.

37. Phase D MUST publish sc-storage, sc-runtime-db-sqlite, sc-config, sc-transport, sc-command, sc-runtime, sc-cron, sc-cron-commands and sc-monty together at version 0.3.0.

38. Phase D MUST retain table-neutral Postgres and MySQL engine implementations in the generated template rather than introduce additional published engine crates.

39. CronStorage MUST NOT expose a public raw-write supertrait or method that bypasses active-name admission, schedule-row limits or generation fencing.

rationale.text: Typed rows and one atomic operation let application and cron policies use each engine without carrying SQL across backends. A single SQLite writer preserves serialized write ownership and reply-after-commit behavior while asynchronous callers remain nonblocking.

positive: Application and cron storage use one contract and the same selected database implementation.
Cron policy is implemented once above table-neutral engines.
negative: The coordinated 0.3.0 release changes legacy storage APIs and requires the beads-cache migration.
Postgres/MySQL engine fixes require template updates and regeneration because their implementations remain generated in this phase.
neutral: Synchronization and unspecified permission behavior remain outside Phase D.

groups.name: Separate cron database and write path
groups.description: Keep cron persistence independent of application storage.
pros: Retains the existing cron-specific storage API.
cons: Separates application and schedule rows and duplicates storage ownership.
groups.why_rejected: It does not meet the shared application-database and single-writer requirements.

groups.name: Retain separate generated SQLite and cron storage implementations
groups.description: Keep the generated SQLx SQLite store alongside the cron SQLite implementation.
cons: Retains multiple write mechanisms and table-specific storage paths.
groups.why_rejected: It does not provide one interchangeable typed storage contract or the required SQLite writer path.

decisions.title: Shared command transforms and one Monty implementation

context.text: CLI, HTTP and MCP must share the same application command behavior. The common path needs a default conversion for simple commands and a replaceable transform for application rules. Monty execution must be reusable without cron, and scheduler hooks and command transforms must share the interpreter implementation.

decision.text:
1. CLI, MCP and HTTP interfaces MUST invoke the same application command read and write paths through the daemon.

2. The daemon command path MUST be reachable over HTTP through a Unix-domain socket or TCP transport.

3. sc-command MUST provide asynchronous storage_read(store, transform, key) and storage_write(store, transform, input) functions over Storage<T>.

4. Command failures MUST return typed StorageCommandError values.

5. A command with directly convertible Tcli and Tsql types MUST use built-in conversion and storage behavior without requiring an application-written transform or storage action.

6. Application business rules MUST enter the shared path through the open Transform seam.

7. Cron command storage MUST use the sc-cron-commands policy adapter to CronStorage without exposing its raw backend or duplicating cron policy.

8. Documentation MUST identify Transform, storage_read and storage_write as provisional in version 0.3.0.

9. The command seam MUST permit later addition of a second transform input, a typed Ok outcome that writes nothing distinct from Err, and a transform within an atomic transaction without breaking consumers.

10. Those three deferred command-seam behaviors are outside Phase D implementation scope; this does not prohibit later addition.

11. The Phase D interpreter transform MUST complete before the storage transaction begins.

12. Monty compilation, sessions, resource limits, host-function dispatch, typed interpreter errors and session dump/load MUST be implemented only in sc-monty.

13. sc-monty MUST expose a compiled session and value-level MontyInvoke<Tin,Tout> invocation of a script and named function with typed inputs and output.

14. At d-5 closure, sc-monty normal and build dependencies MUST be limited to pydantic Monty crates, excluding sc-*, Tokio and serde_json.

15. At d-5 closure, sc-monty source and tests MUST NOT define cron types, cron-reserved names or a copied scheduler/store implementation.

16. Interpreter extraction MUST begin with an exact copy of the current sc-cron code, dependencies and unit/integration tests that passes before any API change.

17. The passing baseline commit MUST remain reachable from the d-5 closing commit.

18. Interpreter separation MUST preserve every copied assertion.

19. sc-cron MUST call sc-monty for interpreter execution while retaining its own cron policy and JSON/value conversion.

20. Monty cron hooks MUST receive values rather than JSON strings.

21. Monty command transforms MUST call sc-monty directly with source read at invocation from an application-owned UTF-8 file configured at daemon setup.

22. Transform source replacement MUST take effect without rebuilding the application.

23. Transform source file-read and UTF-8 errors MUST return typed transform failures.

24. The bounded interpreter execution adapter MUST keep blocking interpreter work off Tokio request workers.

25. The interpreter execution adapter MUST NOT block storage submission.

26. Generated applications MUST be able to select Monty without selecting cron.

27. The template widget create and delete commands MUST use storage_write.

28. The template widget get command MUST use storage_read.

29. cron.start and cron.end MUST use storage_write.

30. cron.list MUST use storage_read.

31. The Phase D user commands cron.start, cron.end and cron.list MUST use the shared command path.

32. cron.start MUST allow the configured application transform to modify or append user JSON before schedule persistence.

33. Command-path requirements MUST NOT mandate hand-written code or prohibit a later consumer-side generator against the delivered framework.

34. storage_read and storage_write MUST own conversion, transform invocation and error composition so applications do not duplicate that pipeline.

35. Only cron command storage MUST use the library policy adapter; ordinary application commands use the default store path without an additional application-written storage action.

rationale.text: Library-owned read/write composition removes repeated pipelines while preserving the application transform seam. Separating the interpreter from cron makes it available to no-cron applications and prevents multiple hosts from diverging. Provisional extensible interfaces preserve later command shapes without implementing them in this phase.

positive: All three interfaces invoke the same application behavior.
Simple commands need no custom transform or storage action.
Cron and command transforms share one interpreter implementation.
negative: Interpreter extraction must preserve both generic and cron-specific assertions across the package boundary.
The command seam remains provisional in 0.3.0.
neutral: Consumer-side generation and unspecified interface permission differences remain follow-up work.

groups.name: Separate interface-specific storage paths
groups.description: Implement read/write composition independently in CLI, HTTP and MCP handlers.
cons: Duplicates transforms and storage behavior across interfaces.
groups.why_rejected: It does not satisfy the shared command-path requirement.

groups.name: Cron-local interpreter with a second transform host
groups.description: Keep Monty implementation in sc-cron and add another host for command transforms.
pros: Avoids extracting the current interpreter implementation.
cons: Duplicates compilation/session/host behavior and couples interpreter reuse to cron.
groups.why_rejected: It violates the single-Monty implementation and no-cron reuse requirements.

decisions.title: `OpError` is built on `sc-observability-types`

context.text:
`sc-command` (directory `crates/sc-command`) defines the sc-ai-cli response
envelope `Envelope<T>`, a JSON object with keys `version`, `ok`, `data`,
`error`, and the typed error `OpError` with fields `kind`, `code`, `message`,
`details` and `suggested_action`.

The SC logging stack already publishes the types for a stable error code and
for remediation guidance in the crate `sc-observability-types` 1.5.0:
`ErrorCode`, a string newtype, and `Remediation` with `RecoverableSteps`.
Logs and diagnostics use them. The problem is that if `sc-command` defined its
own versions, the same failure could carry one code in an API response and
another in the log, and there would be two definitions to keep in step.

Pulling against that: the library crates in this repository do not depend on
the logging runtime `sc-observability`, so that each stays usable in a
program with no SC logging
([ADR-RUN-0004](../architecture.md) makes the project's `main.rs` initialise
observability directly).

decision.text:
2026-10-31 amendment: [ADR-RUN-0017](../architecture.md#adr-run-0017-initial-release-observability-shim)
adds only the command-owned canonical port and foreign EventError signature.
It explicitly supersedes the exact-pin rejection below for the temporary
registry types `=1.5.0` bridge; initial locks prove 1.5.0, while 1.5.1 is
capability-gated future cleanup. Event/error value identity remains upstream.

`OpError.code` is `sc_observability_types::ErrorCode` from
`sc-observability-types` under temporary exact registry
requirement `=1.5.0` (ADR-RUN-0017).
`sc-command` defines no error-code type and no remediation type of its own.
`OpError.remediation` is `Option<sc_observability_types::Remediation>`.
`None` is the empty variant. A custom serializer writes the wire key
`suggested_action` as a JSON string or as JSON `null`. The tagged
`Remediation` object is never the wire form. `details` is
`Option<serde_json::Value>` and is JSON `null` when absent. Both keys are
always present. `sc-command` does not convert `OpError` to or from
`sc_observability_types::Diagnostic`.

The string is the first recovery step of `Remediation::Recoverable` when
that step is non-empty. Later steps stay off the wire. An empty step list,
an empty first step, and `Remediation::NotRecoverable` write JSON `null`,
never `""`. A not-recoverable justification is copied into wire `details`
under `justification`: the serializer inserts that key into a JSON object,
and wraps any other JSON value as
`{"value": <details>, "justification": <text>}`. Deserializing a non-empty
string builds a one-step `Recoverable`. Deserializing `null` or `""` builds
`None`. A single-step recoverable value with a non-empty step round-trips.
A multi-step value and a `NotRecoverable` value do not round-trip as the
same Rust variant. The JSON produced by the first serialization does
round-trip. REQ-CMD-0002 keeps `suggested_action` a string or `null` and
keeps the error object to those five keys, so this ADR does not add a
`recoverable` flag or a `remediation_steps` list. `NotRecoverable` is null
on `suggested_action` so an agent does not execute the justification.
This closes EXT-005.

`ErrorKind` is `#[non_exhaustive]`. The wire spellings are `invalid_input`,
`not_found`, `conflict`, `unavailable`, and `internal`. An unrecognised
spelling fails deserialization with `ENVELOPE.DISCRIMINANT`. HTTP status is
400, 404, 409, 503, and 500 in that order. That table lives only in
`ErrorKind::http_status_code`. The `server` conversion passes the `u16` to
`StatusCode::from_u16` and uses 500 when the number is not a status code.
The first three kinds are caller errors. The last two are internal errors.
`ErrorKind::all` returns `&'static [ErrorKind]`. The `ENVELOPE.KIND.*`
codes in the inventory below name the mapping in this ADR. They are
documentation of the mapping. They are not a public method and they are not
emitted. The service chooses `OpError.code`. A project that needs another
HTTP status builds the response itself. A later variant stays
source-compatible for downstream `match` because the enum is
`non_exhaustive`, and older decoders still reject the new spelling.
This closes EXT-002, EXT-007, and EXT-008.

`OpError` implements `Display` as `{code}: {message}` and
`std::error::Error`. `ErrorKind` implements `Display` as its wire spelling.
This closes EXT-006.

`Envelope<T>` is the enum `Success { version, data }` or
`Failure { version, error }` with a custom serde map of exactly `version`,
`ok`, `data`, and `error`. `OpError` is a custom serde map of exactly
`kind`, `code`, `message`, `details`, and `suggested_action`. Constructors
write version `"1"`. Deserialization keeps the version it read. That string
does not select a different key set. A contradictory or missing
discriminant, an unknown envelope or error key, or a value of the wrong
JSON type is a serde error whose message includes `ENVELOPE.DISCRIMINANT`.
Unknown fields inside `data` and inside `details` stay lossless
([REQ-CMD-0006](requirements.md)). Unknown keys of the envelope object and
of the error object stay rejected ([REQ-CMD-0001](requirements.md)). The
charter's additive-field upgrade path conflicts with that requirement.
This ADR keeps the requirement. A new envelope or error key is a new
contract, and every consumer upgrades together. `Envelope::into_result`
consumes the value and returns `Result<T, OpError>`, dropping `version`.
This closes EXT-001 and EXT-010.

`IntoMcp` is sealed by a private supertrait and is implemented only for
`Result<T, OpError>`. `into_mcp` takes `self` by value. The trait also
requires `Sized`. Dispatch is static. `dyn IntoMcp` is not a supported API.
Serialization failure does not panic: the HTTP conversion returns status 500
with the body of `Envelope::failure` for an `OpError` whose code is
`ENVELOPE.SERIALIZATION`. A static JSON body with the same four keys is
used only when that envelope itself fails to serialize. `into_mcp` returns
`Err` of rmcp's `ErrorData` (imported by tools as `McpError`). This closes
RBQA-F002. The single status table closes RBQA-F001. The shared
`require_exact_keys` helper closes RBQA-F003.

`OpError::from_transport_strings(code, endpoint, cause, suggested_action)`
builds an `OpError` from those plain strings. It does not depend on
`sc-transport`. The code `DAEMON.NOT_RUNNING` uses
`ErrorKind::Unavailable` and the message `the daemon is not running`.
Any other code uses `ErrorKind::Internal`, keeps that code as `ErrorCode`,
and sets `message` to `transport failure {code} at {endpoint}: {cause}`.
`endpoint` and `cause` are stored in `details` for every code.
`suggested_action` is the caller's already-rendered recovery text. `None`,
or text that is empty after trimming, leaves remediation unset. The crate
does not write a placeholder application name. The application name and the
daemon verb are caller policy. This closes EXT-003.

`sc-command` depends on `sc-observability-types` as an ordinary,
non-optional dependency, temporarily exact `=1.5.0` under ADR-RUN-0017.
This inspected validator/types boundary intentionally rejects consumers that
require newer types until coordinated cleanup; it is a conscious exception
to the earlier caret-only decision. It does not depend on
`sc-observability` or on `sc-observability-otlp`. `sc-command` remains the
only library using its error/remediation surface. `sc-runtime` and `sc-cron`
also depend on the types crate, but only for injected canonical logging;
`sc-config` and `sc-transport` do not. This closes EXT-004.
The logging runtime stays forbidden on all library crates.

Library wire-failure inventory:

These rows are `sc-command`'s own wire failures. Widget create and get, and
every other application operation code, are not rows.

| Failure | Stable code | Cause | Recovery | Docs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Invalid or contradictory envelope discriminant | `ENVELOPE.DISCRIMINANT` | `ok` disagrees with `data` or `error`, a required key is missing, an unknown envelope key is present, or a key has the wrong JSON type | Send `version`, `ok`, `data`, and `error`. Success sets `error` to JSON `null`. Failure sets `data` to JSON `null`. | [REQ-CMD-0001](requirements.md) |
| Serialization failure | `ENVELOPE.SERIALIZATION` | `T`'s `Serialize` implementation returned an error | Return a payload that serializes to JSON. The HTTP edge responds 500 with this code and does not panic. The MCP edge returns rmcp `ErrorData` internal error carrying this code and does not panic. | [REQ-CMD-0004](requirements.md), [REQ-CMD-0005](requirements.md) |
| `ErrorKind::InvalidInput` | `ENVELOPE.KIND.INVALID_INPUT` | Caller error. The service still chooses `OpError.code`. | HTTP 400. Fix the request. | [REQ-CMD-0004](requirements.md) |
| `ErrorKind::NotFound` | `ENVELOPE.KIND.NOT_FOUND` | Caller error. The service still chooses `OpError.code`. | HTTP 404. Use an id that exists. | [REQ-CMD-0004](requirements.md) |
| `ErrorKind::Conflict` | `ENVELOPE.KIND.CONFLICT` | Caller error. The service still chooses `OpError.code`. | HTTP 409. Reload and retry the write. | [REQ-CMD-0004](requirements.md) |
| `ErrorKind::Unavailable` | `ENVELOPE.KIND.UNAVAILABLE` | Internal error. Includes `DAEMON.NOT_RUNNING` from `from_transport_strings`. | HTTP 503. `suggested_action` is the caller-supplied string when one was passed. | [REQ-CMD-0004](requirements.md) |
| `ErrorKind::Internal` | `ENVELOPE.KIND.INTERNAL` | Internal error. The service still chooses `OpError.code`. | HTTP 500. Read `message` and `details`. | [REQ-CMD-0004](requirements.md) |

v0.1 does not define a crate error enum. The only fallible public function
is `IntoMcp::into_mcp`, whose error type is rmcp's, the recorded exception.

rationale.text:
If `sc-command` defined its own versions, the
same failure could carry one code in an API response and another in the log,
and there would be two definitions to keep in step.

consequences.text:
An error code is the same value, of the same type, in an envelope and in a
log record. `sc-command` must follow `sc-observability-types` releases: a
breaking release there is a breaking release of `sc-command`, because
`ErrorCode` appears in its public API. A program that uses `sc-command` but
no SC logging still compiles `sc-observability-types`, which is small.

groups.name: Local copies of the code and remediation types inside `sc-command`
groups.why_rejected: two definitions of the same concepts would drift, and projects would write conversions between them at every logging call.

groups.name: Depending on the full `sc-observability` crate
groups.why_rejected: it would pull the logging runtime into every CLI that only parses envelopes, and it would break the rule that these crates do not wrap or depend on observability.

groups.name: Tolerating unknown envelope or error keys, or parking them in an `extra` map
groups.why_rejected: [REQ-CMD-0001](requirements.md) rejects an unknown key so a CLI reprint cannot drop a field the agent did not see. Payload fields inside `data` and `details` stay lossless under [REQ-CMD-0006](requirements.md).

groups.name: Writing a not-recoverable justification into `suggested_action`, or adding a remediation-steps key
groups.why_rejected: the justification is not an instruction, and [REQ-CMD-0002](requirements.md) keeps the wire value a string or `null` on the existing five keys.

groups.name: An exact `=` pin of `sc-observability-types`
groups.why_rejected: Originally rejected because it narrows consumer resolution. ADR-RUN-0017 explicitly accepts that cost temporarily for inspected 1.5.0 validator/identity proof; cleanup removes it.

groups.name: A public `ErrorKind::mapping_code`
groups.why_rejected: the inventory codes above are documentation and are not on the wire.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: The boundary manifest `boundaries/sc-command/sc-command.toml`,
checked by `sc-lint lint sc-boundary --root .` on the workspace.
`allowed_dependents` temporarily includes runtime+cron under ADR-RUN-0017. `allowed_dependencies` includes
`sc-observability-types` and does not treat it as a forbidden edge.
`forbidden_edges` does not name `sc-observability` or `sc-observability-otlp`,
because those crates are not workspace members, and it does not contain

`cargo tree -p sc-command -e normal --prefix none`, with default features and
with `--features server`, may print a `sc-observability-types ` line at the
workspace-lock resolution `1.5.0` under ADR-RUN-0017
and no line beginning with `sc-observability ` or `sc-observability-otlp `
(name then a space). `crates/sc-command/Cargo.toml` lists
`sc-observability-types = "=1.5.0"` under `[dependencies]` for the bridge
without `optional`.
`axum` is optional at 0.8.9 with `default-features = false`.
A test binds `OpError`'s `code` to `sc_observability_types::ErrorCode`, and
a test asserts that a supplied suggestion serialises as a JSON string
([REQ-CMD-0002](requirements.md)).

architecture_decisions.note: 2026-10-31 amendment

decisions.title: REST and MCP edges are conversions, not wrappers

context.text:
Every REST handler and every MCP tool in a generated daemon must answer with
the response envelope `Envelope<T>` (JSON keys `version`, `ok`, `data`,
`error`). Service functions return `Result<T, OpError>`. Something has to
turn that result into an axum response and into an rmcp tool result.

A framework could do this by supplying its own handler type, extractor,
middleware layer or attribute macro that produces envelopes. The governing principle of this
repository is that the framework builds parts and the project wires them in
ordinary Rust ([ADR-RUN-0001](../architecture.md)), and the repository
admits no macro system and no wrapper around an axum or rmcp type
([NFR-RUN-0003](../requirements.md)).

decision.text:
2026-10-31 bounded exception: ADR-RUN-0017 allows only the neutral
CanonicalLog event-receiver trait in `observability`. It adds no REST/MCP
handler, extractor, middleware, router or framework dialect. All conversion
and handler prohibitions below continue to apply.

`sc-command` reaches both edges through three trait implementations on its
own and standard types, and nothing else:

| Conversion | Feature | Used as |
|---|---|---|
| `impl<T> From<Result<T, OpError>> for Envelope<T>` | default | `result.into()` as the last expression of an axum handler that returns `Envelope<T>` |
| `impl<T: Serialize> axum::response::IntoResponse for Envelope<T>` | `server` | applied by axum to the handler's return value |
| extension trait `IntoMcp`, method `into_mcp()`, implemented only for `Result<T, OpError>` where `T: Serialize`, sealed by a private supertrait, taking `self` by value. Dispatch is static. `dyn IntoMcp` is not a supported API. | `server` | `result.into_mcp()` as the last expression of an rmcp `#[tool]` function |

Handlers are ordinary axum handlers registered with `utoipa-axum`; tools are
ordinary rmcp `#[tool]` functions.

Because the conversions are implementations of, or feed, third-party
contracts, their signatures are dictated by axum and rmcp:
`IntoResponse::into_response` is infallible, and `IntoMcp::into_mcp` returns
`Result<CallToolResult, McpError>` with rmcp 3.7's `rmcp::ErrorData` (the
name tools import as `McpError`). These two signatures are the recorded
exception to the repository rule that a fallible public function returns a
typed error enum owned by its crate ([ADR-RUN-0006](../architecture.md),
[NFR-RUN-0009](../requirements.md)); that rule applies to errors a crate
itself originates. v0.1 does not add an `sc-command` error enum. Serialization
failure uses those two recorded signatures.

`sc-command` MUST NOT define: a handler type or trait; an axum extractor
(`FromRequest` or `FromRequestParts` implementation); a tower `Layer` or
`Service`; a procedural or declarative macro; a newtype or struct that wraps
an axum or rmcp type; a router, registry or list of operations.

rationale.text:
Any of those
would sit between the project and axum or rmcp: the project would write
handlers in the framework's dialect, and axum and rmcp documentation would
no longer describe the project's code.

consequences.text:
A generated handler body is one line,
`service::create_widget(&s, input).await.into()`, and a tool body is
`service::create_widget(&self.stores, input).await.into_mcp()`. A project
that wants a different response shape on one route does not call the
conversion and returns any axum response it likes; nothing in `sc-command`
or `sc-runtime` notices. Because nothing is applied automatically, a handler
that forgets `.into()` and returns a bare type is not caught by this crate;
keeping the three surfaces in step is left to lint tooling.

groups.name: An attribute macro that generates the handler and the tool from a service function
groups.why_rejected: it is a macro system to maintain and to learn, and it hides the axum and rmcp code the project is meant to own.

groups.name: An envelope extractor or a middleware layer that wraps every response
groups.why_rejected: it wraps axum's types, applies to routes that may not want the envelope, and has no equivalent on the rmcp side, so the two edges would work differently.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: `arch-qa` architecture review of `crates/sc-command/src`
against the MUST NOT list in the Decision: no `proc-macro = true` in
`crates/sc-command/Cargo.toml`; no `macro_rules!`; no `impl` of
`FromRequest`, `FromRequestParts`, `Layer`, `Service` or `Handler`; no
struct with a field of an axum or rmcp type. The same review applies the
repository rule against wrappers and macro systems
([NFR-RUN-0003](../requirements.md)). The template's example handler in
`daemon/src/routes.rs` and tool in `daemon/src/mcp.rs` end in `.into()` and
`.into_mcp()` respectively.

decisions.title: The `server` feature gates axum and rmcp

context.text:
Two programs use `sc-command`. The daemon needs the envelope types plus the
conversions into an axum response and an rmcp tool result, which require
axum and rmcp. The CLI needs only `Envelope<T>` and `OpError`, to parse the
daemon's answer and print it for `--json`; a CLI binary must link none of
axum, rmcp or sqlx, because that would multiply its build time and binary
size. One published crate has to serve both.

decision.text:
Phase C extends the existing feature separation with optional independent
schema, using probe-frozen schemars/Utoipa identities for owner-local schema
traits on canonical Envelope<T>/OpError/ErrorKind. Schema enables neither
server nor scheduler, and defaults select neither feature. The manually owned
Envelope schema matches its existing custom success/failure serialization;
no wrapper DTO or generic response schema is introduced. C-1 owns only the
narrow compileable declaration/manifest baseline before c-3's later migration;
c-6 preserves/tests it and c-4 proves actual typed wire/schema parity. All
ordinary error/conversion rules remain governed by ADR-CMD-0001/0002.

2026-10-31 amendment: ADR-RUN-0017 adds `test-util = []`, off by default
and independent of `server`; it exposes std-only recorder/rejector doubles.
The public canonical port/Noop is unconditional. Exact bridge types pin is
`=1.5.0`; verify isolated default/test-util/cron consumers do not activate server.

In `crates/sc-command/Cargo.toml`, `axum` and `rmcp` are `optional = true`
dependencies enabled only by the feature `server`. `server` is not a default
feature.

`impl IntoResponse for Envelope<T>` and the `IntoMcp` trait with its
implementation are compiled only under `#[cfg(feature = "server")]`.
Everything else (`Envelope<T>`, `OpError`, `ErrorKind`,
`From<Result<T, OpError>>`) compiles with default features.

With default features the crate's direct dependencies are `serde`,
`serde_json`, and `sc-observability-types` at temporary exact requirement
`=1.5.0` under ADR-RUN-0017. `server`
adds `axum` 0.8.9 and `rmcp` `~3.7` and nothing else.
`axum` is declared with `default-features = false`. The conversion uses
`IntoResponse`, `Body`, and `http`. Axum's default features stay off so a
daemon does not enable `form`, `query`, or `tower-log` through feature
unification with this crate. `rmcp` is already `default-features = false`.
`serde_json` is a direct dependency because `details` holds arbitrary JSON.
This closes EXT-009.

Within this repository `sc-runtime` depends on `sc-command` with `server`
enabled. In a generated project the `cli` crate and the `service` crate use
`sc-command` with default features (`service` returns `OpError`; `cli`
parses `Envelope<T>`), and the `daemon` crate needs the `server` conversions
(its handlers return `Envelope<T>` and its tools call `into_mcp()`). The
generated workspace's crate graph is owned by
[REQ-RUN-0301](../requirements.md) and
[ADR-RUN-0303](../architecture.md); this ADR does not decide it.

The generated `service` crate takes `sc-command` (default features) as a
direct dependency, because it may not depend on `sc-runtime`.

rationale.text:
The repository-level decision
is that server-side code in `sc-transport` and `sc-command` sits behind a
cargo feature named `server`, off by default
([ADR-RUN-0003](../architecture.md)).

consequences.text:
The crate is two build configurations, and CI builds and tests both:
`cargo test -p sc-command` and `cargo test -p sc-command --features server`.
A mistake in gating shows up as axum or rmcp in the CLI's `cargo tree`.
Cargo unifies features across a workspace build, so the property "the CLI
links no axum or rmcp" is defined for the CLI built as its own selection
(`cargo build -p cli`), and evidence must come from `cargo tree -p` on the
CLI crate or on `sc-command` alone, not from a whole-workspace build.
neutral:
OPEN: Whether the generated `daemon` crate takes `sc-command` as a direct
dependency with `features = ["server"]`, or reaches it through a re-export
from `sc-runtime`, is not decided. A re-export would have to be added to the
public surface of `sc-runtime`. Once decided in
favour of direct dependencies: the generated `daemon` is the only generated
crate that enables `server`.

OPEN: Under `cargo build --workspace` cargo unifies features, so the CLI
is built against a `server`-enabled `sc-command`. Whether workspace-wide
builds are exempt from the property, or the crates must instead be split
into client and server crates, is not decided; it is recorded on
[NFR-RUN-0001](../requirements.md) and
[ADR-RUN-0003](../architecture.md) and is to be measured by the spike.

groups.name: A separate `sc-command-server` crate holding the two conversions
groups.why_rejected: Rust's orphan rule forbids implementing axum's `IntoResponse` for `Envelope<T>` outside the crate that defines `Envelope<T>` without a wrapper type, and it would double the crates to publish and version. (The feature-unification OPEN above may reopen a client/server split; the orphan-rule obstacle would then have to be solved first.)

groups.name: No gating, with axum and rmcp as ordinary dependencies
groups.why_rejected: every CLI would link the server stack.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: `cargo tree -p sc-command -e normal --prefix none` with
default features printing no line beginning with `axum ` or `rmcp ` (name
then a space), and with `--features server` printing a line beginning with
each; `just test`, which runs `cargo test -p sc-command` and
`cargo test -p sc-command --features server`
([REQ-RUN-0004](../requirements.md)). `sc-lint-boundary` is not part of this
enforcement: its manifest format has no cargo-feature key, so it checks
inter-crate edges and the public facade list only and cannot express "axum
only with `server`".

decisions.title: `sc-config` returns `ConfigError` values and never panics

context.text:
`sc-config` (`crates/sc-config`) is the standalone configuration crate: it
reads JSON files, applies environment-variable overrides, and deserialises the
result into the caller's serde type. A program calls it first in `main`,
before logging or any other error reporting is initialised. Its failures are
user mistakes, such as a typo in a JSON file or a missing file, far more often
than bugs. The design states that every `sc-config` method returns a discriminated
union, in Rust an enum such as `Result<T, ConfigError>` with a typed error
enum, and that there are no panics. The design also limits the crate's
dependencies to `serde` and `serde_json`, which rules out error-helper crates.

decision.text:
1. Every public function and method of `sc-config` that can fail returns
   `Result<T, ConfigError>`.
2. `ConfigError` is one public enum, written by hand in `crates/sc-config`.
   It implements `std::fmt::Debug`, `std::fmt::Display` and
   `std::error::Error` without a derive macro from another crate.
3. Decided in this document: `ConfigError` has a distinct variant for each
   of: `default.json` missing; a
   file that exists but cannot be read; a file that is not valid JSON; an
   environment override whose key path passes through a non-object value; the
   merged document failing to deserialise into the caller's type.
4. Each variant carries, as typed fields, the file path or the environment
   variable name at fault ([REQ-CFG-0004](requirements.md)).
5. No code reachable from the public API panics. The repository rule
   ([NFR-RUN-0009](../requirements.md)) applies with no commented-exception
   allowance: no `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!`, `unreachable!`, `todo!`,
   `unimplemented!`, or panicking `[]` indexing, reachable from a public
   function.
6. Stricter than the repository rule, decided in this document: `sc-config`
   also bans `assert!`, `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!` in code reachable from a
   public function, and non-test code reads the process environment with
   `std::env::vars_os`, not `std::env::vars`, which panics on a variable that
   is not valid Unicode.
7. `thiserror` and `anyhow` are not dependencies of `sc-config`.
8. `Loader::new` only stores a validated `AppName`, a directory, and the
   caller's environment pairs, so it returns `Loader`. `AppName::new` can
   fail and returns `Result<AppName, ConfigError>`. Only operations that can
   fail return `Result` ([NFR-CFG-0001](requirements.md)).
9. `sc_config::AppName` uses the shared predicate: ASCII `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`,
   `-`, and `_`, length 1 through 64 bytes. Display is `as_str` or
   `AsRef<str>`. The type does not implement `Deref`. Invalid names are
   `APP.INVALID_NAME`.

Error inventory. One row per `ConfigError` variant. The cause payload is the
variant's typed fields. Path, line, and column stay on the variants that
carry a source location.

| Failure mode | Stable code | Cause payload | Recovery steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Application name rejected at construction | `APP.INVALID_NAME` | `InvalidName.name`, the rejected string | Use 1 to 64 bytes of ASCII letters, digits, `-`, and `_`. |
| `default.json` is absent | `CFG.MISSING_DEFAULT` | `MissingDefault.path`, the full path looked up | Create that file and load again. |
| A present file cannot be read | `CFG.READ` | `Read.path` and `Read.source` (`std::io::Error`) | Make the file readable, or replace a directory at that path with a file. |
| File content is not valid JSON, including non-UTF-8 | `CFG.PARSE` | `Parse.path`, `Parse.line`, `Parse.column`, and `Parse.message` | Fix the JSON at that line and column. The file must be UTF-8. |
| Override path is empty or walks through a non-object | `CFG.OVERRIDE` | `Override.variable`, the full variable name | Drop the empty segment, or change the name so the path does not descend through a scalar, array, or null. |
| Merged document does not match `T` | `CFG.DESERIALIZE` | `Deserialize.message`, `Deserialize.files`, and `Deserialize.variables` | Align the merged JSON with `T`. The listed files and variables are the inputs that were applied. |
| Prefix-matching environment entry is not Unicode | `CFG.NON_UNICODE` | `NonUnicode.variable`, the name as `OsString` | Use a Unicode name and value. Names that do not start with the prefix are ignored. |

rationale.text:
A panic at that point prints a Rust backtrace that tells the user
nothing about which file to fix, and an agent driving the program cannot parse
it.

consequences.text:
- The `main.rs` of a generated project matches on the result of
  `sc_config::load(AppName::new("my-app")?)`, prints the error, and returns an exit code. It
  needs no panic handler.
- Callers can branch on the variant, for example to treat a missing
  `default.json` differently from a malformed one.
- The hand-written `Display` and `Error` implementations cost a few dozen
  lines. That cost is what keeps the dependency list at two crates.
- Adding a failure mode later means adding a variant, which is a breaking
  change for callers that match exhaustively.

groups.name: `thiserror` to derive `Display` and `Error`
groups.why_rejected: it adds a third dependency and a proc-macro compile step to save a few dozen lines for one enum.

groups.name: `anyhow::Error` as the public error type
groups.why_rejected: it is opaque, so a caller cannot branch on the failure or read the file path as data, and it is also an extra dependency.

groups.name: Panicking on a missing `default.json`, on the grounds that the program cannot continue anyway
groups.why_rejected: whether to continue is the caller's decision, and a panic before logging exists is the least diagnosable failure a program can have.

grep patterns and malformed-input tests; the `rust-best-practices-agent`
review agent (`.claude/agents/rust-best-practices-agent.md`) checking for
panicking constructs and opaque error types in the public API.

decisions.title: Merge layers as `serde_json::Value`, deserialise once

context.text:
`sc-config` (`crates/sc-config`) builds one configuration from three layers,
lowest precedence first: `config/default.json` (checked in),
`config/local.json` (gitignored, optional), and environment variables. The
result must be the caller's own serde type, for example a generated project's
`AppConfig` struct. The design fixes the layers and the JSON format. It does
not say how layers are combined, and it states no naming scheme for the
environment variables. The naming scheme `<APP>__<KEY>__<KEY>` is decided in
this document ([REQ-CFG-0002](requirements.md)). The problem is how to combine
the three layers into one value of the caller's own serde type, which the
design leaves open.

Layering can be done in two places. It can be done on typed structs: each
layer is deserialised into a "partial" version of the caller's type in which
every field is `Option`, and the partials are merged field by field. Or it can
be done on untyped JSON before any typed deserialisation happens.

decision.text:
1. Each file is parsed into a `serde_json::Value`.
2. The `local.json` value is merged over the `default.json` value as untyped
   JSON: two objects merge key by key, recursively; in every other case the
   upper layer's value replaces the lower layer's value, arrays and `null`
   included ([REQ-CFG-0001](requirements.md)).
3. Each environment override is applied to the same `serde_json::Value`: the
   variable name gives a key path, the variable's value is parsed as JSON or
   else taken as a string, and it is set at that path
   ([REQ-CFG-0002](requirements.md)).
4. The final `serde_json::Value` is deserialised into the caller's
   `T: serde::de::DeserializeOwned` exactly once, with
   `serde_json::from_value`. No layer is deserialised into `T` on its own.
5. `sc-config` defines no schema, no partial-struct trait and no derive macro.
6. The only file format is JSON.

rationale.text:
The typed
route forces every project to write and maintain a second, parallel struct for
each config struct, or forces this crate to ship a derive macro to generate
one.

consequences.text:
- A project's config type is one ordinary `#[derive(Deserialize)]` struct.
  Its serde attributes, `#[serde(default)]` values and any validation in its
  `Deserialize` implementation govern the result.
- `local.json` and the environment may hold any subset of keys, because no
  layer has to be a complete `T`.
- A type error surfaces once, at the end, against the merged document. The
  value's origin is no longer known at that point, so the error cannot name
  the one file at fault. The deserialisation variant of `ConfigError`
  therefore carries the list of files that were read and the names of the
  environment variables that were applied
  ([REQ-CFG-0004](requirements.md)).
- Syntax errors are still attributed exactly, because each file is parsed on
  its own before merging.
- The whole configuration is held in memory as a `serde_json::Value` during
  the load. Config files are small, so this is acceptable.

groups.name: Partial-struct merging
groups.description: Deserialise each layer into an all-`Option` copy of the caller's type and merge field by field.
groups.why_rejected: every project would maintain a parallel struct per config struct, or this crate would need a proc-macro, which breaks the two-dependency limit.

groups.name: A bespoke configuration language with its own layering syntax
groups.why_rejected: it is more code and a new format for users to learn, where JSON plus a merge function does the job.

groups.name: TOML or YAML files
groups.why_rejected: the design specifies JSON, and each would add a parser dependency beyond `serde` and `serde_json`.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: the `arch-qa` review agent (`.claude/agents/arch-qa.md`),
which checks every plan and code change touching `crates/sc-config` against
this decision: one `serde_json::from_value::<T>` call on the merged value, no
per-layer typed deserialisation, no partial-struct trait or macro, no parser
other than `serde_json`. The merge and override unit tests required by
[REQ-CFG-0001](requirements.md) and [REQ-CFG-0002](requirements.md) check the
behaviour.

decisions.title: `sc-config` is synchronous with two dependencies

context.text:
sc-config provides synchronous startup configuration. This phase adds no watcher, reload or change notification; consumers may add async or reload behavior around it without a framework prohibition.

`sc-config` (`crates/sc-config`) is linked into every daemon and every CLI
built on this repository, and is meant to be usable by any Rust program on its
own. It is the first call in `main`. Automatic reloading, change notification
and async interop are wanted eventually. The design lists the crate's dependencies as `serde`
and `serde_json`, states that `sc-observability` and its OTel export crate
(`sc-observability-otlp`) stay independent of `sc-config`, and records the
reload features as a note for later, possibly as a separate
`sc-config-tokio` crate. The problem is how to provide reload, change
notification and async interop later without bringing an async runtime
(`tokio`) and a file watcher into every program that only reads its
configuration once at start-up.

decision.text:
1. The `[dependencies]` table of `crates/sc-config/Cargo.toml` contains
   exactly `serde` and `serde_json`.
2. `sc-config` does not depend on `tokio`, on `sc-observability`, on
   `sc-observability-otlp`, or on any other crate of this workspace
   (`sc-transport`, `sc-command`, `sc-runtime`).
3. The public API is synchronous: no `async fn`, no returned `Future`, no
   spawned thread or task.
4. `sc-config` does not watch files, reload, or notify callers of changes.
5. If reload, change notification or async interop is built later, it goes
   into a separate crate, possibly named `sc-config-tokio`, that depends on
   `sc-config`. `sc-config` never depends on that crate, and these features
   are not added to `sc-config` behind a Cargo feature.
6. `boundaries/sc-config/sc-config.toml` has an empty `allowed_dependents`
   list. `allowed_dependencies` is `serde` and `serde_json`.
   `forbidden_edges` lists workspace-member targets only. This lint tree's
   only workspace member is `sc-config`, so that list is empty.
   `sc-observability-types` and the other crates.io names in the
   [REQ-RUN-0005](../requirements.md) policy table are not members of this
   tree, so they are not manifest edges. `cargo tree -p sc-config -e normal --prefix none`
   is what fails those names. a-2 created the single-member root lint tree
   (`members = ["crates/sc-config"]`). a-5 extends that workspace to four
   members; this crate's manifest stays the one this sprint writes.
   `[public] facade` lists every `lib.rs` export. sc-lint 0.8.0 parses that
   comma-separated list and does not compare it to the crate. The
   `facade-mismatch` fixture under `examples/spike/boundary-proof/` exports
   `present` and `extra` while its facade names only
   `facade_mismatch::present`; `sc-lint lint sc-boundary` on a copy of that
   tree exits 0. `facade_lists_every_export` is the check that this
   manifest stays aligned with `lib.rs`. The process-test helper
   `sc-config-load-helper` is autodiscovered from `src/bin/` in this
   checkout and excluded from the published package. It is not a facade item.

rationale.text:
Building them now would bring an
async runtime (`tokio`) and a file watcher into every program that only reads
its configuration once at start-up, including small CLIs where compile time
and binary size matter.

consequences.text:
- A CLI pays nothing for configuration beyond `serde` and `serde_json`, which
  it already links for its request and response types.
- `load` can be called before an async runtime exists and from inside an
  async `main` alike. A load is a few small file reads, so blocking briefly at
  start-up is acceptable.
- Logging configuration can be read before logging is initialised, because
  this crate does not depend on `sc-observability`. The program passes the
  loaded values to `sc-observability` itself.
- Adding reload later is an additive new crate, not a breaking change to this
  one.
- A program that wants live reload in v0.1 must call `load` again itself.

groups.name: Async and reload support inside `sc-config` behind a Cargo feature
groups.why_rejected: cargo unifies the features of a crate across all packages built in one invocation, so under `cargo build --workspace` one crate enabling the feature would pull `tokio` into every other user of `sc-config` in that build, the CLI included; it also doubles the API surface to test. The same unification applies to the `server` feature of `sc-transport` and `sc-command`. Whether workspace-wide builds are exempt from the rule that a CLI links no server-side dependency, or those crates must be split into client and server crates instead, is recorded as **OPEN** in [NFR-RUN-0001](../requirements.md) and [ADR-RUN-0003](../architecture.md), to be measured by the spike. This ADR does not depend on the outcome: `sc-config` has no such feature either way.

decisions.title: Optional shared protocol and scheduler adapter

context.text:
The problem is that CLI, HTTP and selected MCP need the same start/end/list
cron operation, result and error JSON interface, while default-off generated
configuration must leave core usable alone.

The actual ATM start/end/list API and ADR-069 are behavioral reference only; no ATM-specific identities, lifecycle or grammar are imported.

decision.text:
The adapter owns its schema-trait implementations as well as its sole DTOs.
C-1 commits the optional independent schema feature (schemars JsonSchema and
Utoipa ToSchema) and compileable declarations/manifest/boundary baseline before
parallel consumers. Its existing probe freezes exact identities compatible
with selected RMCP Parameters<T> and runtime Utoipa, satisfying ADR-RUN-0203.
Defaults and CLI select neither schema nor scheduler; schema adds no runtime,
server or scheduling stack. Generated api-types imports these types rather
than violating orphan rules or duplicating a wire model. C-3 owns selected
projection feature activation and typed schema tests using the executor double;
c-6 preserves/tests the declaration surface while implementing behavior; c-4
compares actual tools/list/OpenAPI schemas and canonical fixtures. Canonical
Envelope/OpError wrapping remains unchanged; adapter schema forwards
command/schema, whose owner-local Envelope<T>/OpError/ErrorKind schemas match
custom wire serialization rather than deriving a different enum representation.
The full typed Envelope<CronResponse> family is compiled and fixture-checked
by c-1.

The default library contains sole CronRequest DTO/schema, canonical Envelope
results and object-safe CronExecutor interface (std boxed Future, no cron type).
Feature `scheduler` adds StandardCronExecutor over core-native CronOperations
and explicit ApplicationTargetBindings. It derives a child real-deadline context
from the same stop/admission state in the standard implementation. Consumers
may implement the existing CronOperations or CronExecutor ports for custom
behavior/lifecycle policies, owning their cancellation, joins, authorization
and accurate errors/outcomes. Such replacement does not inherit the standard
cooperative guarantee or remove its safeguards. Existing usage docs contain
a selected-default recipe plus replacement responsibilities; c-4 follows the
recipe using public APIs in generated and registry consumers.
Application bindings authorize Rust/Python/Monty
targets; the library neither starts a mandatory worker nor loads application
config. Generated opt-in composition belongs to daemon/service code; core
runtime remains assembly without cron dependencies. CLI sends the same DTO
used by HTTP/MCP. C-1 freezes exact ports/DTOs, limits, stable codes and canonical
tests/contracts/phase-c dev-only doubles plus existing test-utils context probe.
C-3 prepares injectable projections; c-6 implements against operation doubles
in parallel with c-5 real cron operations. C-4 binds the real selected factory
and root calls and closes composed behavior. No production stub, public testing
API or hidden concrete-Scheduler dependency replaces those ports.

Edges: application→adapter[scheduler]→cron→command (temporary logging port),
adapter→command[default-features=false]. A new
BOUNDARY-sc-cron-commands manifest and existing dependent-list updates are
c-1 deliverables.
