decisions.title: `DaemonBuilder` `run()` is assembly only, in a fixed order

context.text:
The crate `sc-runtime` (`crates/sc-runtime`) is the one place where a
generated project's daemon is put together: singleton lock, stores, router,
listener. An assembly point like this tends to grow into a framework layer
with lifecycle hooks, plugin points and a configurable start-up sequence.

`<instance-root>` is the per-application, per-user directory resolved by
sc-transport, or an explicitly supplied path; its default location is
undecided ([REQ-TRN-0002](../sc-transport/requirements.md)).
The same crate owns the one endpoint resolver that the daemon and the CLI
share ([ADR-TRN-0002](../sc-transport/architecture.md)), so some component of
the daemon has to call it, and the builder has only five methods through
which inputs could arrive.

decision.text:
Phase C narrow public-surface reconciliation: NFR-RT-0001's closed table and
rustdoc criterion include existing run_with_cleanup and the approved bound
receipt alternative run_with_cleanup_and_bound. These remain Ready-only
terminal alternatives through the same runner, with startup/teardown order
and ADR-RT-0005 ownership unchanged. The bound callback observes the owned
Endpoint after bind; it is not a registry, library wrapper, new typestate or
general callback mechanism. The router test utility is the only additional
free function authorized: it is gated by `test-util`, composes existing
middleware on an ordinary Axum router, and adds no builder method, callback,
lifecycle hook, or assembly behavior.

2026-10-31 amendment: ADR-RUN-0017 changes only canonical port ownership
to command for initial release; the existing command edge carries it. No
assembly phase, lifecycle or dependency budget is added. Upstream direct Arc
cleanup is future work.

`DaemonBuilder` uses consuming typestate. The markers are `NeedStores`,
`NeedRoutes`, and `Ready`. `stores` consumes `NeedStores` and returns
`NeedRoutes`. `routes` consumes `NeedRoutes` and returns `Ready`. `run`
exists only on `Ready`. `mcp` is optional and is implemented only on
`Ready`. `logger` is optional on all three states and returns the same state;
it replaces the fixed `sc-runtime` Noop handle and creates no `NeedLogger`
state or run step. The markers are `pub` so the builder can be named across crates.
They are `#[doc(hidden)]` and are not facade items.

`run()` on the builder returned by `Daemon::builder(&sc_transport::AppName, &daemon_config)`
does exactly five things, always in this order:

1. take the `DaemonConfig` the project already loaded;
2. resolve the instance root by calling the `sc-transport` instance-root
   function, then resolve the bind endpoint by calling the `sc-transport`
   endpoint resolver (endpoint resolution completes before the lock);
3. register SIGINT and SIGTERM streams, then take the exclusive lock on
   `<instance-root>/daemon.lock`;
4. call the project's stores closure, then merge the project's
   `utoipa_axum::OpenApiRouter`, the OpenAPI document route, a health route,
   and the rmcp service at `/mcp` if one was given;
5. bind through `sc-transport` last, and serve until SIGINT or SIGTERM. It is
   one `axum::Router`, served unchanged on every listener `run()` binds.

In the daemon, the component that calls the `sc-transport` instance-root
function and endpoint resolver is `run()`; the generated `main.rs` does not,
and `sc-runtime` has no endpoint logic of its own. The `--endpoint` flag
value (parsed by the project's `main`), the configured endpoint and an
explicit instance root reach `run()` inside `DaemonConfig`; the builder gains
no method for them. Honouring `SC_ENDPOINT` through the resolver is not
loading configuration. This paragraph is decided in this document
([REQ-RT-0008](requirements.md)); the design says only that the daemon binds
"through sc-transport".

Endpoint resolution completes before the lock is taken, so an invalid
endpoint does not take the lock or open stores. Signal streams are registered
before bind. The lock is taken before the stores closure is called. Binding is
the last step. A failure in any step returns a `RuntimeError` and no later
step runs.
The builder has no hook, callback, plugin registry or option that inserts
work between steps or changes their order (decided in this document; the
design lists the five steps and calls the crate a bootstrap, not a framework
layer). The caller-facing sequence is consuming typestate. `Daemon::builder` takes
`&sc_transport::AppName` and `&DaemonConfig` and returns a builder on which
`run` is not implemented. `stores` then `routes` consume the builder. `mcp`
and `run` exist only after `routes`. `mcp` is optional and returns the same
ready builder. `logger` is optional before or after either transition and
preserves `NeedStores` -> `NeedRoutes` -> `Ready`. This crate does not define
`sc_runtime::AppName`.

v0.1 binds exactly one listener. `TransportConfig` is `#[non_exhaustive]` and
has no `additional_endpoints` field. `sc-transport` can bind either kind of
listener ([REQ-TRN-0003](../sc-transport/requirements.md)). The resolver
returns one endpoint, and step 5 binds that endpoint.

`DaemonConfig.transport` is `sc_transport::TransportConfig`.
`DaemonConfig.endpoint_flag` is `Option<String>`. `run` calls
`sc_transport::resolve_endpoint_from_env`, which reads `SC_ENDPOINT`. The
name does not appear in this crate ([REQ-RT-0008](requirements.md)).

rationale.text:
Two repo-level decisions rule that out. The framework instantiates parts and
the project wires them in ordinary Rust, with no registry and no wrapper
types ([ADR-RUN-0001](../architecture.md)). The daemon is the only process
that opens the local database, guarded by an OS lock on
`<instance-root>/daemon.lock` ([ADR-RUN-0201](../architecture.md)), so
start-up order is a safety property and not a preference.

consequences.text:
Start-up behaviour is identical in every project and can be read in one
function. A second daemon on the same instance root never opens the database,
and no request is accepted before the stores and routes exist. A project that
needs work between steps does it inside its own closure: for example, extra
start-up work goes in the stores closure, and extra routes or middleware go
in the routes closure. The crate cannot serve a project that needs a
different order; that project assembles its daemon by hand from `sc-transport`
and `sc-command`.

groups.name: Lifecycle hooks
groups.description: (`on_before_bind`, `on_after_stores` and similar)
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because each hook is framework API a project must learn, and the project's own closures already give it a place to run code at each stage.

groups.name: A plugin registry
groups.description: In which components register themselves with the daemon
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it puts a framework-owned abstraction between the project and axum and rmcp, which the repo-level decision forbids.

groups.name: A configurable step order
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because lock-before-stores and bind-last are safety properties; making them configurable makes them breakable.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: the step-order and failure-stops-later-steps tests required
by [REQ-RT-0001](requirements.md); the explicit-instance-root and
endpoint-override tests of [REQ-RT-0008](requirements.md), and its check that
`grep -rn "daemon\.sock\|127\.0\.0\.1" crates/sc-runtime/src` prints no
line outside test code; `arch-qa` architecture review of the public surface
of `DaemonBuilder` (exactly `stores`, `routes`, `mcp`, `logger`, `run`,
`run_with_cleanup`, `run_with_cleanup_and_bound`; terminal runs are Ready-only).

Amended by: ADR-RT-0005 for the additive ready-state cleanup boundary.

decisions.title: Daemon singleton by `fd-lock` on `daemon.lock`

context.text:
Only one daemon may run per instance root.
`<instance-root>` is the per-application, per-user directory resolved by
sc-transport, or an explicitly supplied path; its default location is
undecided ([REQ-TRN-0002](../sc-transport/requirements.md)).
Tests supply a tempdir. The limit exists because the daemon is the only process
allowed to open the local database and SQLite allows one writer. Singletons
are commonly implemented with a PID file or by probing the listening port.

decision.text:
`sc-runtime` takes an OS exclusive file lock, using the `fd-lock` crate, on
the file `<instance-root>/daemon.lock`. The lock is taken in `run()` before
the project's stores closure is called and before any listener is bound, and
is held for the life of the process. If the lock is already held, `run()`
returns the "lock held" variant of `RuntimeError` without waiting: the
attempt is a non-blocking try-lock (decided in this document; the design
states the exclusive lock but not whether the attempt waits). The crate
writes no PID file and probes no port.

rationale.text:
A PID file goes stale when the process crashes, and PIDs are reused. Probing
a port or socket races: two daemons can both probe, both see nothing, and
both start. Both need clean-up code that does not run on a crash.

consequences.text:
The kernel releases the lock on any exit, including a crash or `kill -9`, so
there is nothing to clean up and the file `daemon.lock` may stay on disk.
Holding the lock proves no other daemon for this instance root is alive, but
it does not prove ownership of an overridden endpoint outside that root.
`sc-transport` therefore acquires and retains a separate endpoint-scoped lock
before replacing a stale Unix socket
([REQ-TRN-0004](../sc-transport/requirements.md),
[ADR-TRN-0006](../sc-transport/architecture.md)). The instance lock remains
earlier because it protects stores; the endpoint lock protects the selected
listener path. The instance guarantee covers the local instance root only; a shared Postgres store may still be written by daemons on several hosts. File-lock semantics on network
filesystems are weaker, so an instance root on such a filesystem is not
protected.

groups.name: PID file
groups.description: A file holding the daemon's process id, checked at start.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it goes stale after a crash and PID reuse makes the check unreliable.

groups.name: Port or socket probing
groups.description: Try to connect, and start only if nothing answers.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because two starters race, and a hung daemon looks absent.

groups.name: A lock inside the database
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it requires opening the database first, which is exactly what a second daemon must never do, and because `sc-runtime` has no database dependency.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: the two-daemon test required by
[REQ-RT-0002](requirements.md): a second `run()` on the same instance root
returns the "lock held" error and its stores closure never runs.
`crates/sc-runtime/Cargo.toml` lists `fd-lock`.

related_documents.text: Source: sc-runtime design, 2026-09-19, section "Runtime architecture"

architecture_decisions.note: Amended by: ADR-RT-0005 for the additive ready-state cleanup boundary.

decisions.title: The project's `Stores`, router and rmcp service pass through

context.text:
See the note on [REQ-RT-0003](requirements.md): opaque `Stores` is the current design, and where the shared command path lives is undecided.

A generated project has one or two stores, each a project-owned crate bound
to one sqlx driver (SQLite, Postgres). `sc-runtime` sits between the code
that opens those stores and the routes and MCP tools that use them.
The problem is which side opens the stores: if `sc-runtime` constructed
them itself it would need a sqlx dependency, knowledge of each backend, and
an opinion about how many stores a project has.

decision.text:
`Stores` is a generic type parameter of the builder. Its value is produced by
the project's stores closure and handed only to the project's routes closure
and optional MCP closure. `sc-runtime` never reads a field of it, calls a
method on it, or requires a trait describing its contents. The
`utoipa_axum::OpenApiRouter` returned by the routes closure and the rmcp
Streamable HTTP service returned by the MCP closure are mounted as they are,
without being wrapped in an `sc-runtime` type. `sc-runtime` adds no MCP
session store or other session state; running the rmcp service in stateless
mode is configured by the generated project's `mcp::service`
([REQ-RUN-0302](../requirements.md)). Opening pools and running
migrations happen inside the project's closure. API names are illustrative
until the contract sprint pins them.

Phase C MCP input clarification:

The ordinary project-supplied StreamableHttpService enters through `.mcp(...)`.
Private middleware retains original JSON POST bytes in an HTTP extension under
the service's own max_request_body_bytes. The read-only `mcp_request_body` accessor
reads those bytes from ordinary request Parts, preserving headers and the absolute
deadline; GET/SSE are untouched. NFR-RT-0001 records this one minimal free function.
Runtime owns no protocol DTO, duplicate-key policy or cron dependency. The generated
cron tool reparses its sole canonical CronRequest from the original generic RPC
envelope before executing. Duplicate struct fields remain rejected by the DTO,
while arbitrary Value payloads and unrelated tools keep their own JSON semantics.
Normal serde_json is removed; test-only parsing is a dev dependency. No extra
public test middleware helper, RMCP wrapper or command registry is introduced.

rationale.text:
If it
constructed the stores itself it would need a sqlx dependency, knowledge of
each backend, and an opinion about how many stores a project has. The
repo-level decision is that the framework instantiates and the project wires,
with no wrapper around an axum, rmcp or sqlx type
([ADR-RUN-0001](../architecture.md)).

consequences.text:
`sc-runtime` has no sqlx dependency, and a project with no database at all
can use it (for example with `Stores = ()`). Which route uses which store
stays entirely in project code. The crate cannot offer store-aware features
such as a database health check or a migration command; a project adds those
in its own router. The health route `sc-runtime` mounts therefore reports on
the process only.

groups.name: A `Store` trait the framework calls
groups.description: (for example `open`, `migrate`, `health`)
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it makes the framework define what a store is and forces every project store to fit it.

groups.name: Built-in pool construction
groups.description: From config inside `sc-runtime`
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it requires a sqlx dependency and per-backend code in this crate, and sqlx requires one crate per database for checked queries.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: the `forbidden_edges` entry `sc-runtime -> sqlx` in the
boundary manifest under `boundaries/sc-runtime/`, checked by
`sc-lint-boundary` through `just lint`; `cargo tree -p sc-runtime -e normal
--prefix none` printing no line beginning with `sqlx ` or `sqlx-`
([NFR-RT-0002](requirements.md)); the opaque-`Stores` tests required by
[REQ-RT-0003](requirements.md); `arch-qa` review that no public type wraps an
`axum`, `rmcp` or `sqlx` type.

related_documents.text: Source: sc-runtime design, 2026-09-19, section "The crates" (`Stores` is a plain struct defined by the project); applies repo [ADR-RUN-0001](../architecture.md)

decisions.title: `DaemonFixture` runs the real daemon

context.text:
Generated projects test each operation through REST, MCP and the CLI client.
Test fixtures often take a shortcut, such as calling the axum router
in-process with no listener.
The problem is that such fixtures skip the lock, the bind, the transport and
shutdown, so tests drift from production behaviour without anyone noticing.

decision.text:
`sc_runtime::testing::DaemonFixture` starts a daemon through the same
`Daemon::builder()` path as production, on a fresh temporary directory used
as the instance root, with a real `daemon.lock`, a real listener bound
through `sc-transport`, and a real `sc_transport::Client` connected to it.
There is one daemon per fixture and one fixture per test. There is no
in-memory or listener-less mode. The name is illustrative until the contract
sprint pins it.

The design states only that the fixture starts a daemon on a tempdir instance
root per test so tests run in parallel. The following points are decided in
this document:

1. the fixture exposes a connected `sc_transport::Client`;
2. the fixture also exposes its resolved endpoint in the string form accepted
   by `--endpoint` and `SC_ENDPOINT`, and its instance-root path, so a test
   can point an MCP client at it, or, on an isolated machine, the CLI binary;
3. one fixture per test, and no in-memory mode;
4. the fixture stops its daemon through a crate-private trigger that runs the
   same shutdown sequence a signal starts
   ([REQ-RT-0005](requirements.md)), never a process signal and never a
   public builder method;
5. dropping the fixture stops the daemon, and drop (or an explicit async
   shutdown) returns only after the listener is closed.

On Windows the fixture does not invent an endpoint. The caller sets
`endpoint_flag`, `transport.endpoint`, or `transport.tcp_port` before
`start`. A fresh temporary instance root still isolates the lock file. The
fixture module is behind the non-default `test-util` feature.

rationale.text:
Such tests skip the lock, the bind, the
transport and shutdown, and drift from production behaviour without anyone
noticing. A single daemon shared by all tests in a binary avoids the start-up
cost but makes tests share a database and a socket, so they cannot run in
parallel or in isolation.

consequences.text:
Every test exercises lock, bind, transport and shutdown. On platforms whose
default endpoint is a Unix domain socket (macOS and Linux), each fixture has
its own instance root and so shares no socket, lock or database file with any
other, and fixtures run in parallel in one test binary. On Windows the lock
and database files are isolated the same way. Endpoint isolation on Windows
is the caller's endpoint value. Each fixture costs a tempdir and a
socket, which is cheap enough for that. A bug in start-up or shutdown shows
up as a failure in many tests at once, which is the intended signal.

groups.name: An in-memory router mode
groups.description: That calls the router with no listener
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it skips lock, bind, transport and shutdown, the parts most likely to differ between test and production.

groups.name: One shared daemon per test binary
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because tests would share state and a socket, could not run in parallel safely, and would break the repo-level rule that every test uses its own tempdir instance root.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: `req-qa` requirements review of the tests required by
[REQ-RT-0006](requirements.md), in particular the concurrent-fixtures test,
the `SC_ENDPOINT` child-process test and the stop-one-of-two test;
inspection that `DaemonFixture` calls `Daemon::builder()` and has no separate
serve path.

decisions.title: Await application cleanup before releasing runtime ownership

context.text:
An application can start a background worker from its existing stores closure
after the runtime acquires `daemon.lock`. The SDK must provide a general cleanup boundary without
importing cron or choosing application policy.

decision.text:
NFR-RT-0001's exact seven-method surface includes this existing cleanup
terminal method and the bound-receipt alternative alongside run. All three
are Ready-only alternatives through the same runner, as reconciled in
ADR-RT-0001; no extra setter, registry, wrapper or callback engine is added.

Phase C target amendment (planned): REQ-RT-0006's additive portable
`DaemonFixture::start_with_cleanup` reuses this production ownership sequence
and common internal fixture runner; ordinary start uses empty cleanup. Preserve
once-only cleanup, primary startup error, stores/logger/instance-lock lifetimes,
endpoint ordering and physical fixture-thread join. REQ-RT-0005 additionally
selects Windows Ctrl-Break with early registration/polling alongside Ctrl-C;
Unix and private fixture triggers remain unchanged. No alternate lifecycle or
public test shutdown trigger is introduced.

The Phase C production bound-endpoint callback delegates through this same
runner and preserves the existing transport port-zero ownership handshake.
One actual Endpoint callback while the listener is retained supports isolated
real-signal test IPC; it is not a health signal. No reserve/drop/rebind helper,
retry/sleep workaround, new transport API or alternate lifecycle is introduced.

1. The ready-state `DaemonBuilder` adds `run_with_cleanup(cleanup)`, with
   `FCleanup: FnOnce() -> Cleanup` and `Cleanup: Future<Output = ()>`. It
   consumes the same ready builder as `run()`. Existing `run()` delegates with
   empty cleanup. No cleanup hook exists on earlier builder states; no startup
   hook, registry, JobContext, or new startup phase is introduced.

2. The    existing startup order remains unchanged: take the loaded
   configuration,    resolve instance/endpoint, register signal streams, acquire
   the singleton    lock, invoke the application stores closure, then assemble
   and bind the    existing router/MCP service. The cleanup extension does not
   inspect project    `Stores` or wrap routes or services.

3. When awaited normally, cleanup runs    exactly once after serving/listener
   disposal, including typed startup and    serving failure paths. Unused
   startup closures are dropped before early-error    cleanup, so cleanup may
   await ownership sent by a stores closure without an    unused SDK-held sender
   keeping its channel alive.

4. Any acquired instance    lock, the successful `Stores` owner, and the
   retained runtime logger remain    alive through cleanup. Teardown order is
   application cleanup, retained    `Stores`, instance lock, retained runtime
   logger, then return the original    `RuntimeError` or success. Cleanup
   returns unit and does not replace that    primary result.

5. The application owns worker drain/join and concrete logger    shutdown. The
   SDK has no cron dependency, logger wrapper, secret provider, or
   application policy. The application consumes concrete logger shutdown only
   after the runtime and cleanup return and their shared handles drop.

6. The    caller must await the run future to completion. Dropping/canceling the
   future    or panicking inside cleanup cannot promise asynchronous cleanup.
   Deadlines    bound cooperative work; arbitrary native code or synchronous
   operations    cannot be forcibly preempted. Ownership must be joined before
   claiming    cleanup completion, even when a cooperative deadline was missed.

rationale.text:
Releasing that lock when HTTP serving
stops, before the application joins its worker, permits a replacement daemon to
start overlapping work.

consequences.text:
This explicitly amends ADR-RT-0001's no-callback restriction only for the
additive ready-state cleanup boundary and ADR-RT-0002's lifetime-of-the-process
wording: on an awaited run, the instance lock is retained through cleanup and
released before that run returns, after the successful stores owner is dropped.
Other startup and builder decisions remain in force. ADR-RT-0003's project
`Stores`/router/service pass-through is unchanged. The original typed errors and
application-owned observability lifecycle remain unchanged.

A replacement daemon started on the same instance root while cleanup runs
returns `LockHeld` and does not run its stores closure, so it cannot start a
worker that overlaps the draining one. Because the lock attempt does not wait,
that replacement fails instead of queuing and must be started again after
cleanup returns. Cleanup that is blocked on native or synchronous work past
its cooperative deadline keeps the instance lock held until that work is
joined. Each application writes its own worker drain/join and concrete logger
shutdown, and must await the run future to completion.

groups.name: Release the instance lock when HTTP serving stops
groups.description:
The runtime releases `daemon.lock` as soon as HTTP serving stops, before the
application joins the worker it started from the stores closure.
groups.why_rejected:
Rejected because a replacement daemon could then acquire the lock and start
overlapping work while the old worker is still draining.

groups.name: Lifecycle hooks or a registry
groups.description:
A startup hook, a cleanup hook on an earlier builder state, a registry or a
JobContext through which the application registers its worker with the runtime.
groups.why_rejected:
Rejected because ADR-RT-0001 rejects lifecycle hooks and a plugin registry;
cleanup is instead one Ready-only terminal method.

groups.name: SDK-owned worker drain and logger shutdown
groups.description:
The SDK imports cron, drains and joins application workers itself, and shuts
down the concrete logger through a wrapper.
groups.why_rejected:
Rejected because the SDK must provide a general cleanup boundary without
importing cron or choosing application policy.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: the runtime lifecycle regressions in
`crates/sc-runtime/src/tests/lifecycle.rs`, including retained successful
stores/lock/logger during cleanup, replacement-daemon rejection until cleanup
returns, and early unused-closure disposal; the generated production composition
and cron worker/store ownership regressions. [REQ-RT-0001](requirements.md),
[REQ-RT-0002](requirements.md), and [REQ-RT-0005](requirements.md) retain their
startup, singleton, and graceful-shutdown obligations.

related_documents.text: Source: B18 corrective lifecycle integration; preserves the existing startup contract and application-owned workers/logger.

decisions.title: Client uses reqwest `unix_socket`, no custom connector

context.text:
The client half of the crate `sc-transport` (`crates/sc-transport`) sends
HTTP requests from a CLI to a local daemon. On macOS and Linux the default
transport is a Unix domain socket (UDS); on Windows and for cross-host use
it is TCP. Most Rust HTTP clients historically spoke only TCP, so an early
draft of this project assumed HTTP over a Unix socket needed the
`hyperlocal` crate or a hand-written hyper connector. That is no longer
true: reqwest 0.13 provides `ClientBuilder::unix_socket(path)`.
The problem is that the client needs HTTP over UDS on macOS and Linux and
over TCP elsewhere, and the project prefers standard crates used the
documented way over code it must own.

decision.text:
The client in `sc-transport` is a plain `reqwest::Client` from reqwest 0.13.
For a UDS endpoint it is built with
`reqwest::ClientBuilder::unix_socket(path)`. For a TCP endpoint it is built
normally and requests go to the base URL `http://<ip>:<port>`.
`crates/sc-transport/Cargo.toml` does not depend on `hyperlocal`. The crate
contains no type that implements a hyper or tower connector trait and no
code that writes or parses HTTP on a raw stream.

The client speaks plaintext `http://` only. `reqwest` is built without a TLS
feature, so `rustls` is not in the graph. Adding TLS later is a new feature,
not a default cost.

`Client::new(Endpoint)` stays the handoff constructor. v0.1 connect and
request timeouts are each two seconds, and the client has no header map.
That limit is not the permanent contract. The extension point is a future
`#[non_exhaustive] ClientOptions` and `Client::with_options(endpoint, options)`.
`Client::new` remains and uses the default options. Timeouts and default
headers are added on `ClientOptions`. v0.1 does not define that type.
A caller with a longer operation waits for that type; it does not fork the
client to set a timeout.

Error inventory:

Every `TransportError` variant is a `Result` value. `code()` returns the
stable code and is the source of truth; the `code` field is informational
and `code()` does not read it. Each struct variant is `#[non_exhaustive]`.
Variants that carry `cause` return that `TransportCause` from `Error::source`.
`TransportCause` is not a second `Result` error. a-6 maps the code to
`ErrorCode` and owns `suggested_action`. This crate carries neither.

| Variant | Failure | Stable code | Payload | Recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `InvalidName` | `AppName::new` rejected the string | `APP.INVALID_NAME` | `name`, `detail` | `detail` says empty, longer than 64 bytes, or which character was outside ASCII `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `-`, `_` |
| `InvalidEndpoint` | Endpoint text did not parse | `TRANSPORT.INVALID_ENDPOINT` | `source`, `detail` | Use `uds:<path>` or `tcp:<socket-addr>`. An empty string is invalid |
| `MissingTcpPort` | Windows default has no `tcp_port` | `TRANSPORT.MISSING_TCP_PORT` | `code`, `detail` | `detail` says to set `TransportConfig.tcp_port` or pass a `tcp:` override. This crate has no default port |
| `InstanceRootUnavailable` | Per-user base directory is missing | `TRANSPORT.INSTANCE_ROOT_UNAVAILABLE` | `detail` | Set `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or `HOME` on Unix, or `LOCALAPPDATA` on Windows, or pass `TransportConfig.instance_root` |
| `DaemonNotRunning` | UDS path missing, or the connection was refused | `DAEMON.NOT_RUNNING` | `code`, `endpoint`, `cause` | Report the code, endpoint, and cause. `Error::source` is the cause. The variant has no `suggested_action`, no `AppName`, and no `ErrorCode`. This crate does not name `daemon start` |
| `ResponseDecode` | The body is not `T` | `TRANSPORT.RESPONSE_DECODE` | `status`, `cause`, `body_preview` | `body_preview` is a lossy UTF-8 prefix of at most 512 bytes. Read `status`, `cause`, and that preview. A body that is `T` is `Ok(T)` at every HTTP status |
| `TimedOut` | The 2s connect or request timeout elapsed | `TRANSPORT.TIMED_OUT` | `endpoint`, `cause` | v0.1 timeouts are fixed. The extension point is `ClientOptions` above. This is neither `DaemonNotRunning` nor `ResponseDecode` |
| `Request` | Other client failure, including a directory path and a UDS endpoint on non-Unix | `TRANSPORT.REQUEST` | `endpoint`, `cause` | Correct the endpoint. This is not a down-daemon signal |
| `Bind` | The listener could not bind | `TRANSPORT.BIND` | `endpoint`, `cause` | Free the address or create the parent directory. This crate does not create it |
| `UnsupportedEndpoint` | UDS was requested on non-Unix | `TRANSPORT.UNSUPPORTED_ENDPOINT` | `endpoint`, `cause` | Use a `tcp:` endpoint. Unix domain sockets are not available on this platform |
| `EndpointBusy` | Another listener holds the endpoint lock | `TRANSPORT.ENDPOINT_BUSY` | `endpoint`, `cause` | Leave the live socket in place |
| `NotASocket` | The UDS path exists and is not a socket | `TRANSPORT.NOT_A_SOCKET` | `endpoint`, `cause` | The path is left unchanged |

rationale.text:
The project
prefers standard crates used the documented way over code it must own.

consequences.text:
One well-known HTTP client serves both transports, and the UDS path adds no
code beyond one builder call. `unix_socket` exists only on Unix, so there is
no UDS client on Windows; that is why the Windows default endpoint is TCP on
`127.0.0.1`. The crate is tied to reqwest 0.13 or later.

groups.description: A crate that adds a Unix-socket connector to hyper.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it is an extra dependency and a lower-level client API for something reqwest now does itself.

groups.name: A bespoke hyper connector
groups.description: A type written in this crate that opens a `UnixStream` for hyper.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it is custom code to write, test and maintain where a standard tool already does the job.

`hyperlocal`; `reqwest` at `0.13` with `json` and without `rustls`);
`cargo tree -p sc-transport -e normal --prefix none`, with and without
`--features server`, printing no line beginning with `hyperlocal ` or
`rustls ` (the name followed by a space). The same check is the
`dependencies` integration test. The `arch-qa` review agent checks the
source for a custom connector or hand-written HTTP.

decisions.title: One endpoint resolver shared by daemon and CLI

context.text:
A daemon and its CLI are separate binaries. The CLI must find the address
the daemon listens on with no coordination at run time: there is no
registry process to ask. The address can come from several places: a
`--endpoint` command-line flag, the `SC_ENDPOINT` environment variable, the
project's configuration, or a platform default. Tests
and multi-instance setups also need to move both binaries to another
address with one setting.

decision.text:
The crate `sc-transport` exposes `resolve_endpoint(&AppName, flag: Option<&OsStr>, environment: Option<&OsStr>, &TransportConfig)`. The daemon binary and the CLI binary both call it, or they call `resolve_endpoint_from_env`, which reads only `std::env::var_os("SC_ENDPOINT")` and then calls `resolve_endpoint`. It returns a UDS path or a TCP socket address, taken from the first of these sources that supplies a value:

1. the `--endpoint` flag value, parsed by the calling binary and passed in;
2. the value of the `SC_ENDPOINT` environment variable, passed in as an
   explicit input;
3. the endpoint from the caller's configuration, passed in;
4. the platform default: UDS at `<instance-root>/daemon.sock` on macOS and
   Linux; TCP on `127.0.0.1` with the port from configuration on Windows.

`<instance-root>` is the per-application, per-user directory from
`instance_root(&AppName)`, or `TransportConfig.instance_root` used
unchanged. On Unix the default base is non-empty `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`,
otherwise `$HOME/.local/state`. On Windows the base is `LOCALAPPDATA`. The
path is `<base>/<app>`. `instance_root` does not create the directory.

Further decision points:

5. The resolver accepts the `SC_ENDPOINT` value as an explicit input. A
   convenience form may read the variable itself, only with
   `std::env::var_os("SC_ENDPOINT")`, and then calls the explicit form.
   Decided in this document.
6. Who calls the resolver. In a CLI, the `cli` crate's own code calls it
   with the parsed `--endpoint` value, the `SC_ENDPOINT` value and its
   configuration ([REQ-RUN-0310](../requirements.md)). In a daemon,
   `sc_runtime`'s `run()` calls the instance-root function and the resolver
   and has no endpoint logic of its own; the daemon's `main.rs` puts the
   parsed `--endpoint` value, the configured endpoint and any explicit
   instance root into `DaemonConfig`, which carries them to `run()`
   ([REQ-RT-0008](../sc-runtime/requirements.md)). No other code in the
   daemon, the CLI or `sc-runtime` computes an endpoint.
7. The endpoint and instance-root portion of configuration is one public
   `serde::Deserialize` type exported by `sc-transport` with default
   features. A CLI cannot name `sc_runtime::DaemonConfig` because a CLI does
   not depend on `sc-runtime`, so the shared type lives here. The type is
   `TransportConfig`. It is `#[non_exhaustive]`. Its fields are
   `endpoint: Option<String>`, `instance_root: Option<PathBuf>`, and
   `tcp_port: Option<u16>`. It has no `additional_endpoints` field.
   v0.1 binds exactly one listener for one config. A later dual-bind adds a
   field on this type. v0.1 does not ignore a reserved value. a-5 embeds
   this type and does not decide a second shape. `DaemonConfig` embeds
   `TransportConfig`; the surrounding `DaemonConfig` field names stay with
   [REQ-RT-0001](../sc-runtime/requirements.md).
8. TCP ports come from project configuration (or from an explicit
   override). Port ranges are allocated per project in the central port
   registry kept in the synaptic-canvas repository. No TCP port is
   hard-coded in the crates of this workspace or in the template.
9. On Windows, a platform default with no `tcp_port` is
   `TransportError::MissingTcpPort`. An override that names `uds:<path>`
   still resolves to a UDS endpoint. Use of that endpoint on Windows fails
   in `Client::new` or `bind`.
10. v0.1 of this crate binds exactly one listener per `TransportConfig`.
    `bind` may still be called twice by a caller that already has two
    endpoints. The transport dual-bind question is closed.
    `sc_runtime::Daemon::builder()` remains owned by sc-runtime. a-5 copies
    this decision into the root documents.

The order of sources 1 to 3 is decided in this document; the sc-runtime
design names the sources but not their precedence. The Windows address
`127.0.0.1` is stated by the design; that the Windows port comes from
configuration is decided in this document.

rationale.text:
If each binary combined
those sources with its own code, they could disagree and never meet.

consequences.text:
Agreement between daemon and CLI is structural, not a convention to
remember. An override works identically on both sides, which tests and
multi-instance setups rely on. The crate does not parse command lines or
load configuration, so it needs neither `clap` nor `sc-config`; the calling
binary passes those values in. A user who sets `SC_ENDPOINT` for the CLI but
not for the daemon will still get a mismatch; the resolver cannot prevent
different inputs.
neutral:
OPEN: Whether v0.1 of the template renders a default TCP port into a
generated project's configuration is not decided
([REQ-RUN-0301](../requirements.md)). This crate does not close that point.

groups.name: Discovery files
groups.description: The daemon writes its address to a file that the CLI reads.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it adds state that goes stale after a crash, and the file's own location would still need a shared resolver.

groups.name: Port scanning
groups.description: The CLI probes a port range for the daemon.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it is slow, unreliable, and does not apply to UDS.

groups.name: Separate client and server defaults
groups.description: Each binary holds its own default logic.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because the two copies can drift apart, which is the exact failure this decision removes.

given the same inputs meet; and a text search, done by the `arch-qa` review

anywhere.

decisions.title: Response types and `OpError` mapping belong to the caller

context.text:
Two facts pull `sc-transport` toward knowing the types of the crate
`sc-command`. First, the CLI example in the sc-runtime design receives an
`Envelope<Widget>` from `client.post(...)`, and `Envelope<T>` is defined in
`sc-command`. Second, `DAEMON.NOT_RUNNING` is an error code in the sc-ai-cli
error convention, whose error type `OpError` is also defined in
`sc-command`.

decision.text:
Amended: 2026-10-23 by sprint a-3. `DaemonNotRunning` carries `code`,
the endpoint, and the cause. Sprint a-1 (2026-10-24,
[ADR-RUN-0004](../architecture.md)) kept the code a `&'static str`.

1. The `sc-transport` client methods `get` and `post` are generic over the
   response type `T: serde::de::DeserializeOwned`. The caller names the
   type, for example `Envelope<Widget>`. `sc-transport` never names
   `Envelope` or `OpError`.
2. `TransportError::DaemonNotRunning` is `sc-transport`'s own typed error
   variant. It carries `code: &'static str`, exactly `DAEMON.NOT_RUNNING`,
   the endpoint, and the cause. It carries no `suggested_action`, no
   `AppName`, no `sc_observability_types::ErrorCode`, and no `Remediation`.
   This crate does not name `daemon start`. The error-inventory table under
   ADR-TRN-0001 lists every variant.
3. Converting that code plus endpoint and cause into an `OpError` (including
   `ErrorCode` and `suggested_action`) is owned by `sc-command` as a published
   constructor that takes plain strings only, so `sc-command` still does not
   depend on `sc-transport`. The generated `cli` crate (a-6) calls that
   constructor and owns `suggested_action` for every `TransportError`. It
   does not embed a copy of the mapping in `main.rs`.
4. `crates/sc-transport/Cargo.toml` does not list `sc-command`,
   `sc-observability`, `sc-observability-types`, or `sc-observability-otlp`.

The method and type names above are the pinned public contract. This
decision was made in this document; the sc-runtime design does not state
where the mapping lives.

rationale.text:
But the repository rule is that `sc-config`, `sc-transport`
and `sc-command` are standalone crates with no dependency edges among them,
so each can be published and used alone
([ADR-RUN-0003](../architecture.md)). A dependency from `sc-transport` on
`sc-command` would break that rule.

consequences.text:
There is no dependency edge among the standalone crates, and `sc-transport`
is usable by a daemon and CLI pair that does not use the sc-ai-cli envelope
at all. The cost is one published `sc-command` constructor per Phase A
decision, called from the generated CLI. The strings `DAEMON.NOT_RUNNING` and the
`OpError` field layout are defined in two crates that cannot check each
other at compile time.

groups.name: `sc-transport` depends on `sc-command` and returns `OpError` directly
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it adds an edge between two crates that must stay standalone, and forces every user of the transport to take the envelope.

groups.name: A shared types crate that both depend on
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because it is a fifth crate to publish and version for the sake of two strings.

implementation.text:

decisions.title: The `server` cargo feature gates axum and listener binding

context.text:
The crate `sc-transport` has two halves with different users. Listener
binding exists to feed `axum::serve` in a daemon, so it needs axum. Endpoint
resolution and the HTTP client are used by a CLI, and a CLI binary must link
none of axum, rmcp or sqlx: they would multiply its build time and binary
size.

decision.text:
In `crates/sc-transport`, `bind(&Endpoint) -> Result<Listener, TransportError>`
and `Listener` are compiled only under `#[cfg(feature = "server")]`. In
`Cargo.toml` the feature `server` is not in `default`, and `axum` is
`optional = true`, enabled only by `server`. Endpoint resolution, the client
and `TransportError` are in the default build. Within this workspace only
the crate `sc-runtime` enables `sc-transport/server`; a generated `cli` crate
depends on `sc-transport` with default features. `Listener` is one type.
`local_endpoint` reports the bound address, including a TCP port assigned
for port `0`. The `axum::serve::Listener` associated stream and address are
opaque structs with private inners. They are `#[doc(hidden)]` and are not
facade items, because route code must not branch on the transport. Callers
use `Listener::local_endpoint` and `axum::serve`.

`crates/sc-transport/Cargo.toml` is a temporary single-crate workspace
(`[workspace] members = ["."]` plus `[workspace.package]`, with
`Cargo.lock` beside it) so this leaf can build and run
`sc-lint lint sc-boundary --root crates/sc-transport` before a-5 registers
the crate. a-5 deletes that `[workspace]` table, `[workspace.package]`, and
`Cargo.lock` when it adds the member. A package cannot belong to two
workspaces. Do not copy the leaf workspace into a generated consumer.

rationale.text:
Both halves must agree on endpoints, so they belong in one crate. The
repository rule is that server-side code in the standalone crates sits
behind a `server` cargo feature that is off by default
([ADR-RUN-0003](../architecture.md)).

consequences.text:
A CLI that depends on `sc-transport` links tokio and reqwest but not axum.
CI must build and test the crate twice, with and without `server`, because
code behind a feature is otherwise not compiled. Cargo unifies features
across one build, so a workspace build that includes `sc-runtime` will
compile `sc-transport` with `server`, and a CLI built in that same build is
linked against the `server`-enabled crate. The property "a CLI links no
axum" is therefore defined for a CLI built as its own selection
(`cargo build -p cli`), and evidence must come from `cargo tree` on the CLI
or on this crate alone, not from a workspace build.
neutral:
OPEN: Whether workspace-wide builds are exempt from the no-axum
property, or the crate must instead be split into a client crate and a
server crate, is not decided; the spike must measure it. The open point is
owned by [NFR-RUN-0001](../requirements.md) and
[ADR-RUN-0003](../architecture.md).

groups.name: Separate client and server crates (for example `sc-transport-client` and `sc-transport-server`)
groups.why_rejected: Not chosen because it doubles the crates to publish and version, and splits the shared endpoint resolver across crates or forces a third one. It is not equivalent to the feature: a crate split keeps axum out of a CLI even in a workspace-wide build, which the feature does not. It is reconsidered if the OPEN above is resolved against the feature.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: `cargo tree -p sc-transport -e normal --prefix none`
printing no line beginning with `axum ` (the name followed by a space), and
the same command with `--features server` printing one; `just test` running
`cargo test -p sc-transport` and `cargo test -p sc-transport --features
server` ([REQ-RUN-0004](../requirements.md)). The boundary manifest format
has no cargo-feature key, so `sc-lint-boundary` does not enforce this
decision; it enforces only the inter-crate edges of
[NFR-TRN-0003](requirements.md).

decisions.title: Transport access control is UDS file permissions only

context.text:
A daemon built on `sc-transport` serves every operation of an application
over HTTP, so anything that can open a connection to its listener can run
those operations. On macOS and Linux the default listener is a Unix domain
socket (UDS) file at `<instance-root>/daemon.sock`; on Windows, for
cross-host use and for browser frontends it is TCP. `<instance-root>` is the
per-application, per-user directory resolved by sc-transport, or an
explicitly supplied path. On Unix the default base is non-empty
`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, otherwise `$HOME/.local/state`. On Windows the base is
`LOCALAPPDATA`. The path is `<base>/<app>`
([REQ-TRN-0002](requirements.md)). A TCP port has no such
protection: any local process, and for a non-loopback address any host that
can route to it, can connect. The sc-runtime design raises bearer tokens for
TCP listeners, and `Origin` and `Host` header checks on the `/mcp` route, as
ideas only and leaves them out of the build plan. Without a recorded
decision a reader cannot tell whether a TCP listener is meant to be
protected.

decision.text:
1. On a UDS listener the only access control is the permission bits of the
   socket file. After `sc-transport` binds it, the file has no access for
   group and no access for others (`mode & 0o077 == 0`,
   [REQ-TRN-0004](requirements.md)). There is no token, no peer-credential
   check and no header check.
2. A TCP listener bound by `sc-transport` is unauthenticated in v0.1. Any
   process that can reach the address can call the daemon.
3. The only TCP address `sc-transport` computes by default is the loopback
   address `127.0.0.1` (the Windows platform default). Any other TCP address
   is used only when an override (`--endpoint`, `SC_ENDPOINT`) or the
   caller's configuration names it.
4. Bearer tokens for TCP listeners, and `Origin` and `Host` checks on
   `/mcp`, are deferred. v0.1 of `sc-transport` and `sc-runtime` contains no
   such check. Adding one needs a later ADR that names this one.
5. The socket file mode is `0o600`. The mode is set on the socket file only.
   The instance-root directory is left unchanged.

rationale.text:
A UDS file can be protected by ordinary
file permissions, the approach dockerd uses.

consequences.text:
The default transport on macOS and Linux needs no port, no token and no
secret storage, and is private to the operating-system user. On Windows, and
wherever a project configures TCP, every local process of every user can
call the daemon; a project that configures a non-loopback address exposes
the daemon to the network with no authentication, and that is the
project's own decision and risk. A browser page can send requests to a
loopback TCP listener, because no `Origin` or `Host` check exists. These
limits are accepted for v0.1.

groups.name: A bearer token on TCP listeners
groups.description: The daemon writes a secret to a user-only file and the client sends it in a header.
groups.why_rejected: Deferred because it needs token creation, storage and rotation code on both sides, and the default transport does not need it.

groups.name: `Origin` and `Host` header checks on `/mcp`
groups.description: Reject requests that come from a browser page or a rebound DNS name.
groups.why_rejected: Deferred for the same reason; it matters only when a daemon listens on TCP.

groups.name: UDS peer-credential checks (`SO_PEERCRED` and similar)
groups.description: The daemon asks the kernel for the connecting user id.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because file permissions already restrict who can connect, and the call differs per platform.

groups.name: No TCP support until authentication exists
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because Windows has no UDS client in reqwest, so Windows would have no transport at all.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: the permission test of [REQ-TRN-0004](requirements.md)
(criterion 1: `mode & 0o077 == 0` after bind); the Windows default test of
[REQ-TRN-0001](requirements.md) (criterion 5: the address is `127.0.0.1`);
the `arch-qa` review agent checks that `crates/sc-transport/src` and
`crates/sc-runtime/src` contain no token, `Origin` or `Host` check and no
default TCP address other than `127.0.0.1`.

decisions.title: endpoint lock guards UDS replacement and listener lifetime

context.text:
A Unix domain socket (UDS) listener is a file. When a daemon process dies
without cleaning up (a crash, `kill -9`, power loss) the file stays, and the
next attempt to bind the same path fails with "address in use".
But a socket file that exists may also belong to a daemon that is alive, and
removing it cuts that daemon off from every new client. The listener-binding
function of `sc-transport` (`bind(&Endpoint)`, behind the `server` cargo
feature) cannot tell the two cases apart reliably with a connect probe.

decision.text:
1. For a UDS endpoint `S`, `bind` first opens `S.lock` and attempts a
   nonblocking OS-exclusive lock. It performs no inspection or removal of
   `S` unless that lock succeeds. `S.lock` means the literal `.lock` suffix is
   appended to the complete socket path.
2. The returned `Listener` retains the endpoint lock for its lifetime. A
   competing bind that cannot acquire it returns a typed bind error and does
   not unlink, replace, chmod, or clean up `S`.
3. Once the lock is held, `bind` removes an existing stale socket file and
   binds a new socket at `S`. It does not use a connect probe or process
   check. Cleanup removes `S` only while the same listener holds `S.lock`.
   The `S.lock` file is never deleted; only the OS lock is released, avoiding
   an inode-replacement race between old and new contenders.
4. The endpoint lock complements rather than replaces
   `<instance-root>/daemon.lock`: runtime holds its instance lock before
   stores open, then `bind` acquires endpoint ownership immediately before
   touching the selected UDS path.
5. The bind rustdoc states the lock path, retention, replacement, failure,
   and cleanup behavior.
6. This decision is made in this document; the sc-runtime design states
   only that file permissions restrict access to the socket.
7. When the existing path is not a socket, `bind` returns
   `TransportError::NotASocket` and leaves the path in place.

rationale.text:
A daemon
that cannot restart after a crash without manual cleanup is not acceptable.

The runtime's `<instance-root>/daemon.lock` is not sufficient:
two daemons may use different instance roots while an endpoint override makes
them target the same UDS path. Ownership must therefore be scoped to the
endpoint itself and must also protect standalone users of `sc-transport`.

consequences.text:
A daemon restarts cleanly after a crash with no manual step, and endpoint
overrides cannot let a second instance unlink a live listener. The server
feature gains one small locking dependency and `Listener` retains one guard.
The lock, unlink of a stale socket, and permission change run inside
`tokio::task::spawn_blocking` during `bind`, so the async caller does not
stall a runtime worker. Drop of the listener still unlinks the socket
synchronously: `Drop` cannot await, and the unlink must happen while this
listener still holds the lock. A non-transient accept error closes the
inner socket and stops `accept` instead of retrying forever.

groups.name: Connect probe
groups.description: Try to connect to the existing socket and unlink only if the connection is refused.
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because there is a race between the probe and the unlink, a live but overloaded daemon can look dead, and it duplicates a guarantee the singleton lock already gives.

groups.name: Fail with "address in use" and leave cleanup to the caller or the user
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because every restart after a crash would then need a manual step or the same unlink code copied into every caller.

groups.name: Rely only on `sc-runtime`'s instance lock
groups.why_rejected: Rejected because an endpoint override may point two independently locked instance roots at the same socket.

implementation.text:
Enforced by: the stale-socket, competing-owner, rustdoc, cleanup, and
no-probe criteria of [REQ-TRN-0004](requirements.md); on the caller side, the
start-up order of `sc_runtime`'s `run()`, which takes `daemon.lock` before
`bind` acquires endpoint ownership
([REQ-RT-0001](../sc-runtime/requirements.md)).

related_documents.text: Source: decided in this document; the sc-runtime design does not state it
